Using chemogenetic tools, kappa opioid receptor expressing neurons in the preoptic area were activated in mice subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion. Core body temperature, metabolism, infarct volume, and motor recovery were assessed under conditions permitting hypothermia or maintaining normothermia. Untargeted metabolomic profiling was performed on whole brain tissue collected 30 minutes after activation in the absence of ischemia. Activation of kappa opioid receptor expressing preoptic neurons induced a hypothermic state with coordinated metabolic changes, reduced infarct volume and improved acute motor outcomes. These effects were attenuated when body temperature was maintained at normothermia. Metabolomic profiling revealed coordinated alterations in nucleotide, phospholipid, and sphingolipid pathways. These findings link temperature dependent cerebroprotection to coordinated metabolic remodeling, with translational relevance for stroke.

title: Grid cells are not a parsimonious source of the hexadirectional signal
abstract: Hexadirectional modulation is widely treated as a proxy for population-level grid-cell activity in humans. Conventional analyses test the sixth harmonic of the mean directional response, whereas we show grid-cell firing predicts a dominant sixfold modulation of cell-level variance, rather than population-level mean. Using analytical derivations, simulations and recordings from 23,453 rodent medial entorhinal neurons, we show that grid cell tuning alone cannot account for the measured mean signal. Analysis of 1,349 conjunctive grid-head-direction cells revealed insufficient grid-axis alignment and directional tuning specificity to account for population-level hexadirectionality. A hypothetical additional nonlinearity mechanism near the cell level can produce a a small sixfold population-level mean modulation, [≤] 2%, under favorable circumstances. Moreover, the current methodology does not adequately differentiate genuinely symmetric activity and stable directional peaks, nor contextualize a harmonic measurement in a solid spectral framework. These findings show that mean hexadirectional modulation neither follows directly from grid-cell firing nor uniquely identifies grid-cell activity. We provide an improved framework for testing a link between the two in future studies.
author_corresponding_institution: NTNU - Norwegian University of Science and Technology

title: HERO: A hierarchy-aware analysis pipeline for reducing and refining whole-brain atlas-mapped cellular datasets
abstract: Advances in high-throughput mesoscale microscopy and machine learning-based image analysis pipelines have made unbiased whole-brain imaging widely accessible. However, translating the resulting atlas-mapped datasets into biologically meaningful results remains a substantial barrier owing to their sheer magnitude and complex hierarchical organization. Consequently, reporting structure and analysis methods vary widely across studies, undermining rigor and reproducibility. To address this, we developed a user-friendly data reduction workflow, HERO (Hierarchy-aware Expression Region Organization), designed to perform hierarchy-aware selection, refinement, ranking, and visualization of whole-brain cell detection datasets. The workflow is customizable to specific needs, requires minimal coding experience, and outputs transparent, curated results. HERO functions as a seamless plug-in within larger-scale whole-brain cell detection analysis pipelines, providing efficient, unbiased region selection to streamline subsequent statistical analyses and comparative evaluations. Although HERO is developed with mouse cell-detection datasets, it can be applied to any atlas-mapped dataset that contains hierarchical information. Here, we applied the HERO pipeline to example cell detection datasets containing afferent cells from the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and the insular cortex (insula). HERO provided top projecting regions consistent with historical tracing studies for the BST (e.g., amygdalar and hypothalamic regions) and the insula (e.g., somatosensory, autonomic, and interoceptive regions). Furthermore, the refinement step of HERO provides additional enriched regions originally obscured in the primary ranked outputs, such as memory- and emotion-associated structures. With HEROs dynamic processing, we were able to identify top-projecting regions consistent with the literature and, additionally, find regions often obscured in these large datasets. In sum, HERO offers a standardized analysis workflow to reduce whole-brain cell-detection datasets, transforming raw regional cell counts into curated results and advancing the effectiveness, interpretability, and accessibility of whole-brain imaging in neuroscience.
author_corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine

title: Postprandial hypertriglyceridemia activates microglia to promote satiety via an ASC dependent signaling.
abstract: Reactive microglia are commonly considered neurotoxic and detrimental for brain functioning. Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet strongly activates microglia, disrupts the central control of energy metabolism, contributes to obesity, and promotes cognitive decline. In this study we report an unexpected beneficial function of microglia reaction at the time scale of a meal, whereby they promote satiety in a macronutrient-dependent manner. We show that murine microglia react to ingested dietary fat within three hours. Specifically, postprandial hypertriglyceridemia induced microglial hyper-ramification alongside with a transcriptional reprogramming promoting communication with neurons. This effect occurs in discrete brain areas, including the hypothalamus and the brainstem, which control hunger. Remarkably, microglia-specific genetic ablation of Apoptosis-associated Speck-like protein containing a CARD (named ASC), a master regulator of metabolism, immune function and cell shape, profoundly alters satiety following high-fat food consumption. These results reveal that microglia engage an immune signaling pathway to rapidly alert the neural circuits and activate an anorectic response that limits overconsumption of dietary fat. Unexpectedly, this regulatory process is sexually dimorphic, present in males only. Furthermore, we found that the postprandial microglial reaction is bypassed during obesity, providing a new therapeutic target to treat maladaptive eating disorders.

title: Neural Representations of Visual Anagrams in Macaque Inferotemporal Cortex
abstract: Visual recognition requires stable representations of object identity despite large changes in the retinal image. Yet this stability must be selective: some transformations change not only how an image looks, but also what object it appears to depict. Visual anagrams highlight this challenge: a single image can resemble two different objects at different orientations, such as an elephant and a rabbit. Here, we asked how macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex represents such transformations. We recorded large neuronal populations while presenting visual anagrams and unambiguous exemplars of their two interpretations across rotations. Neurons preferring one exemplar tended to prefer anagram orientations supporting the corresponding interpretation. At each of the two interpretation-relevant canonical angles, population responses more closely resembled those to the matching exemplar than those to the nonmatching exemplar. This matching advantage persisted when both exemplars were presented at the alternative canonical angle. Decoders trained exclusively on exemplars across rotations also tracked the shifts in anagram representations. Visual models showed anagram-exemplar alignment as well, with stronger alignment in models with greater relative shape preference. These findings suggest that transformation tolerance in IT is sensitive to what an image appears to depict, while relative shape preference is associated with similar representational organization in visual models.
author_corresponding_institution: Peking-Tsinghua Center for Life Sciences, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China.; School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences, Peking University, Beijing

title: Reaching movements in virtual reality depend on the seen avatar arm and not just the acting arm
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) offers unique opportunities to study behaviour by allowing the visual environment to be manipulated in ways otherwise impossible in the real world. A central theoretical question is how body-related visual information shapes movement control. Given right-handers' greater dexterity with the right arm, perhaps even seeing a right arm vs. a left arm may engage sensorimotor processes associated with more precise motor control. We examined reaching performance while participants used their own right or left arm to move the manipulandum of a KINARM robot to intercept static targets. Participants wore a VR head-mounted display, calibrated to the robot's physical workspace, in which they saw either the right or left arm holding and moving the manipulandum. The 2 x 2 design allowed for independent manipulation of the controlling arm and virtual arm displayed. As expected, reaches were faster and more accurate when controlled by the right arm. More interestingly, performance was also affected by the seen arm. Participants made straighter reaches when they saw a virtual right arm than a left arm, especially for the right controlling arm. These findings show that precise motor control relies not only on the arm that is actually moved and provides proprioceptive feedback, but also on the visual identity of the arm. The ability to modulate performance using visual features in VR opens new theoretical questions and opportunities for applications such as rehabilitation.

title: Recovering Hidden Neural Oscillatory Modes from Partial Observations through Delay Embedding and Perturbation
abstract: Characterising the oscillatory behaviour generated by neural interactions is central to systems neuroscience because these dynamical properties are linked to brain function. However, inferring latent neural dynamics is challenging because recordings sample only part of the system. Time-delay embedding allows dynamical modes to be estimated from partial recordings, using methods such as Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel DMD). Despite its promise, two questions remain: what dynamical information is recoverable through time-delay embedding, and how can recovery be improved? We address both questions using control theory. Our framework centres on factorising the Hankel matrix of delay-embedded observations into an observability matrix and a trajectory matrix with the form of a controllability matrix. We show that their ranks impose complementary constraints on what any delay-embedding method can recover: delay embedding can increase observability rank, while perturbation can increase trajectory rank by exciting otherwise inactive modes. We validate this framework using Hankel DMD in simulations and human electrocorticography (ECoG). In both, perturbation increased the number of fast-decaying mode estimates, whereas greater delay depth increased the number of reliably estimated modes and, in ECoG, extended their frequency range. These results clarify what partial recordings can reveal about neural dynamics and how to reveal more.
author_corresponding_institution: Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, The University of Tokyo

title: A Reproducible Cortical Model of Focal Epileptiform Activity with a Multi-Biomarker Analysis Pipeline
abstract: The development of surface-based therapeutic strategies, including extracranial illumination and epicortical electrical or optoelectronic neuromodulation, requires experimental models in which focal pathological activity can be generated and monitored within an accessible cortical region. Here, we established an acute cortical model of focal epileptiform activity in anesthetized mice based on local microinjection of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) into the barrel cortex. This preparation provides precise spatial and temporal control of the epileptiform focus while enabling simultaneous electrophysiological sampling across cortical depth. To objectively characterize the induced activity, we implemented a Python-based analysis pipeline integrating complementary electrophysiological biomarkers, including oscillatory power, multi-unit activity, pathological fast ripples (250-650 Hz), and epileptiform bursts. Local 4-AP administration produced robust increases in gamma (30-100 Hz) power, multi-unit firing (MUA), fast ripple and burst activity. Pharmacological sensitivity of the framework was evaluated using carbamazepine, which robustly attenuated 4-AP-induced increases in all biomarkers. Together, this study provides a reproducible experimental and analytical framework for investigating focal cortical epileptiform activity and for the future evaluation of pharmacological, optical, and electrical interventions targeting superficial cortical networks.
author_corresponding_institution: Instituto de Investigaciones Biomedicas de Barcelona, CSIC

title: Predicting the Efficacy of Myopia Control Spectacle Lenses by Simulating Their Optical Effect on the Retina
abstract: Slowing myopia progression is central to addressing a growing public health concern. Myopia control spectacle lenses with diverse optical designs have been proposed for this purpose, and show varying degrees of clinical efficacy. Relating their design to their efficacy remains an open challenge. Here we show that it is possible to predict their clinical efficacy from their optical design, by reconstructing their impact on the retinal image. We simulated how several lens designs affect the retinal image using a combined lens and eye optical model. By assuming that the retina extracts specific features from the retinal image to modulate eye growth, we could predict the cumulative absolute reduction in axial elongation (CARE) of lens designs with very different rationales and microstructures. Our results show that different myopia control spectacle lenses can be compared on a common optical basis, and that their efficacy is predictable from their optical properties. This work paves the way for rational design of next-generation lenses and for adapting designs to each patient's ocular optics.
author_corresponding_institution: Sorbonne Université, Institut de la Vision, INSERM, CNRS

title: Dizocilpine-derived K2060 exhibits enhanced blockage at NMDA receptors with impaired Mg2+ block and provides strong protection against audiogenic seizures
abstract: Background and Purpose: Voltage-dependent Mg2+ block is a defining feature of the GluN1/GluN2 subtype of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs). We tested how impaired Mg2+ block at GluN1/GluN2A receptors mutated at the GluN2A-N615 position modifies inhibition by dizocilpine-derived K2060 compared with clinically used memantine and ketamine. Experimental Approach: Electrophysiological recordings were performed on recombinant wild-type (WT) and mutated GluN1/GluN2A receptors expressed in HEK293T cells. Acute hippocampal slice electrophysiology and behavioural studies were conducted in WT and knock-in GluN2A-N615S mice. In vivo tolerability and efficacy were evaluated using open field testing, prepulse inhibition (PPI), and protection against audiogenic seizures (AGS). Key Results: Mg2+ reduced the apparent potency of all three blockers and slowed onset at the GluN1/GluN2A-WT receptor. These Mg2+-dependent effects were absent or markedly reduced at the GluN1/GluN2A-N615S and GluN1/GluN2A-N615K receptors. In addition, K2060 showed slower unbinding and greater trapping than memantine. In hippocampal slices from GluN2A-N615S mice, K2060 exhibited enhanced but slower onset inhibition than memantine and ketamine. In vivo, K2060 caused no overt behavioural disruption at 5 mg/kg (i.p.) and did not further disrupt PPI. All three blockers protected GluN2A-N615S mice against AGS at 5 mg/kg (i.p.); only K2060 remained protective at 1 mg/kg (i.p.). Conclusions and Implications: Impaired Mg2+; block removes a physiological constraint on the action of NMDAR blockers. K2060 exhibited the most favourable pharmacological profile, supporting its further evaluation for studies with NMDAR hyperfunction models. Additional pharmacokinetic, safety, and disease-model studies are warranted.
author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Experimental Medicine of the Czech Academy of Sciences, Department of Neurochemistry, Videnska 1083, 142 20 Prague, Czech Republic

title: The role of world knowledge in sentence comprehension under working-memory constraints: An fMRI study
abstract: Introduction: Comprehension of thematic roles, i.e., "who did what to whom," relies on limited cognitive resources, and constraints on these resources can alter the use of plausibility information derived from world knowledge. Although sentence-processing studies have described how plausibility information constrains interpretation, it remains unclear how this process is supported by the architecture of working memory. This study examines whether the phonological loop, one of the components of working memory, contributes to thematic-role processing based on world knowledge. Methods: Using articulatory suppression and functional magnetic resonance imaging, we examined whether constraining the function of the phonological loop modulates behavioral and neural responses to sentences in which syntactically assigned thematic roles are plausible or implausible given world knowledge. To constrain the phonological loop, we manipulated the task: a single task and a dual task involving concurrent articulation. Results: We found no significant interaction between task and plausibility, although equivalence analyses did not provide evidence for the absence of a plausibility effect during articulation. In contrast, a robust main effect of thematic-role plausibility was observed: implausible sentences elicited greater activation than plausible sentences in the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG) and medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) at the whole-brain level, and in both the pars triangularis and pars orbitalis of the LIFG in the ROI analyses. Discussion: These findings provide no conclusive evidence that constraining the phonological loop substantially modulates the use of world knowledge in comprehension of thematic roles, while also leaving open the possibility of a smaller task-dependent effect. At the same time, the robust neural responses to implausibility indicate that the LIFG and mSFG consistently contribute to the processing of plausibility information derived from world knowledge.

title: Attentional modulation of persistent visual representations after stimulus offset is coordinated across primary visual and anterior cingulate cortices
abstract: Flexible behavior in complex environments requires animals to infer which sensory inputs are relevant for guiding action and which need to be ignored. Yet, how cognitive control circuits apply contextual knowledge during decision-making is poorly understood. To address this question, we trained head-fixed mice on a cross-modal, context-dependent two-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) decision-making task. In this task, animals simultaneously received visual and auditory inputs, and the behaviorally relevant modality switched covertly between blocks of trials, requiring animals to infer rule changes from reward feedback alone. Mice successfully adapted their behavior after rule switches and recovered to expert performance. Using simultaneous Neuropixels recordings in the primary visual cortex (V1) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) during task performance, we found that neuronal responses in both regions showed mixed selectivity, multiplexing sensory, choice, and outcome signals. However, V1 neural responses more strongly encoded visual stimulus orientation, while ACC neural responses preferentially encoded outcome. Population decoding further revealed that V1 and ACC neurons maintained a persistent representation of task context throughout the trial, occupying a subspace approximately orthogonal to visual stimulus coding. This contextual representation strengthened progressively as mice adapted their behavior following each switch. Critically, context representations emerged in parallel in V1 and ACC, and decoding accuracies in these two regions were strongly correlated with each other and with behavioral performance across trial blocks. Orthogonal to this shared emergent and sustained context signal, visual stimulus decoding was enhanced when vision was task-relevant. This attentional enhancement in V1 occurred not only during the stimulus presentation period but also after stimulus offset. Similarly, in ACC, a persistent increase of visual stimulus identity encoding in visually relevant session blocks was present after stimulus offset. Taken together, these findings reveal a distributed, inter-areal representation of task context spanning sensory and frontal cortices, suggesting that V1 and ACC contribute to maintaining task-relevant sensory information beyond the immediate sensory response period to provide a circuit-level mechanism for cross-modal attentional control.

title: Crowding distorts features, not objects: structured target confusions in a 4AFC conjunction task
abstract: Visual crowding is the disruption of peripheral object identification by nearby flanking clutter. It remains unclear whether crowding disrupts the bound representation of an object or degrades the object's component features separately. We addressed this with a 4AFC conjunction-report task in which observers reported both the orientation and the brightness of every target. Target Gabors at 6 degrees eccentricity were presented alone or flanked at 1, 3, or 5 degrees separation by Gabors varying independently in colour and/or orientation similarity to the target. We analysed the data three ways: joint accuracy, accuracy on each feature alone, and the statistical coupling between the two report channels. Orientation reports were principally impaired by orientation-similar flankers within the smallest target-flanker separations, whereas luminance reports were impaired by target-colour-similar flankers across a broader spatial range. Observed joint accuracy was closely predicted by the product of the two marginal accuracies in every condition. A complementary chi-square analysis of the full 4x4 stimulus-response matrices agreed with this conclusion at the most-crowded conditions, while revealing structured response biases that the ratio test could not detect. These biases were present at baseline and were not amplified by crowding. The conjunction errors observed under crowding therefore arose from two largely independent feature-specific failures, rather than from disruption of a representation in which the two features are bound. These results indicate that object-level crowding errors in this paradigm are the downstream signature of two independent feature-level processes rather than the breakdown of an object-level mechanism.

title: The effect of preproenkephalin gene deletion on heart function in mice
abstract: Enkephalins, the endogenous ligands of the - and {delta}-opioid receptors, are abundantly expressed in the nervous system and peripheral organs, including the heart. Accumulating evidence suggests that they participate in cardiac development and act as autocrine and paracrine modulators of heart activity. Here, we investigate the role of enkephalins in cardiac physiology using a newly generated mouse strain with a complete ablation of the preproenkephalin (Penk) gene. We find that, although adult mutant mice weighed less, the mutation caused no apparent changes in behavioral phenotype, no increase in anxiety-like behaviors, and only a mild reduction in locomotor activity. There was no effect of Penk deletion on heart weight or size. A comprehensive analysis of left ventricular function using MRI revealed normal basal cardiac performance, except for a significant reduction in the peak fill and ejection rates. There were no significant effects of Penk deletion on left ventricular function after {beta}1-adrenergic stimulation with dobutamine. At the same time, we observed the expected significant differences in heart size and function between male and female mice. In conclusion, our data show that enkephalins are not essential for normal heart development and have a moderate impact on adult heart function under basal conditions.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Molecular Neuropharmacology, Maj Institute of Pharmacology, Polish Academy of Sciences, Smetna 12, 31-343 Krakow, Poland

title: Separation, isolation, and membrane lipid profiling of selectively vulnerable and resilient neurons
abstract: Certain neurons are more susceptible to pathogenic stressors and degenerate, while others remain resilient in neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms underlying this cell-to-cell heterogeneity in neuronal vulnerability remain unclear, primarily due to challenges in isolating vulnerable and resilient neurons to characterize their properties. In this study, we report the development of a novel cell-labeling method utilizing two cell-impermeable dyes to identify vulnerable and resilient neurons in culture, which are subsequently separated and isolated via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). As a proof-of-concept of a mechanistic study, we conducted lipidomic analysis to determine whether the lipid composition of membranes differs between vulnerable and resilient neurons to oxidative stress. This simple but unique method sets the groundwork for investigating the molecular underpinnings of selective neuronal vulnerability, which could inform new diagnostic strategies and therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.

title: ZFP36 is a post-transcriptional regulator of the P2X4 receptor in myeloid cells
abstract: P2X4 is an ATP-gated purinergic receptor upregulated in spinal microglia after peripheral nerve injury, where it plays a key role in neuropathic pain. Yet, the molecular mechanisms controlling P2X4 expression remain incompletely understood. To address this question, we examined P2X4 mRNA expression and translation in spinal microglia following nerve injury. While total P2X4 mRNA levels remained unchanged, ribosome-associated P2X4 mRNA increased, revealing a previously unrecognized level of translational regulation. We therefore investigated whether the RNA-binding protein ZFP36 (tristetraprolin), a well-established regulator of inflammatory mRNAs, controls P2X4 expression. Our results demonstrate that the P2X4 3'UTR strongly repressed reporter and protein expression and that ZFP36 emerged as a negative regulator of P2X4 mRNA. This regulation involved phosphorylation-dependent signaling through p38 MAPK and 14-3-3. Moreover, ZFP36 knockdown increased P2X4 protein expression, while manipulation of ZFP36 phosphorylation altered P2X4-dependent ATP-evoked calcium responses. Together, these findings identify ZFP36 as a previously unrecognized post-transcriptional regulator of P2X4, extending its role beyond inflammatory mediators to a functional purinergic receptor. They reveal post-transcriptional control of receptor availability as a novel regulatory layer linking myeloid cell state to purinergic responsiveness and provide a new framework for understanding microglial P2X4 regulation in neuropathic pain.
author_corresponding_institution: IGF, Universite de Montpellier, CNRS, INSERM, Montpellier, France

title: Dual Roles of Interferon-γ Receptor in Somatostatin Interneurons at Baseline and During Inflammation
abstract: Background: Neuropsychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder show converging evidence of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) dysfunction, including consistent reductions in somatostatin (SST) interneuron markers. SST interneurons are selectively vulnerable to inflammation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in mood and anxiety disorders, signals through the IFN-{gamma} receptor (IFNGR), which is expressed in neurons. We tested whether IFNGR signaling in SST interneurons regulates anxiety-like and cognitive behavior and prevents inflammation-induced molecular deficits. Methods: We generated mice with conditional deletion of IFNGR from SST cells and assessed anxiety-like behavior using elevated plus maze and working memory using Y-maze at baseline and after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced inflammation. Expression of SST-related, neurotrophic, synaptic, and glial markers was quantified. Results: At baseline and after LPS-induced inflammation, IFNGR deletion in SST cells increased anxiety-like behavior without affecting working memory. In control mice, LPS reduced Sst (p=0.0006), neuropeptide Y (Npy) (p=0.0022), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) (p<0.0001), and synapsin 1 (Syn1) (p=0.0150); these reductions were not significant in mice lacking IFNGR in SST cells. Knockouts also showed lower baseline Bdnf, Syn1, Gephyrin (Gphn), and allograft inflammatory factor 1 (Aif1, encoding Iba1) than controls. Conclusions: IFNGR signaling in SST cells plays a dual role: supporting normal behavior and molecular homeostasis while mediating LPS-induced molecular deficits. These findings link immune signaling to the GABAergic dysfunction implicated in major depressive disorder and suggest IFNGR signaling in SST cells may regulate cortical microcircuit integrity at baseline and during inflammatory challenge.
author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), Toronto, ON, Canada; Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Toronto; Department of Psychiatry,

title: Exploratory Proteomics of Brain Extracellular Vesicle Enriched Preparations After LPS Challenge and miRNA Associated Vesicle Administration
abstract: We used brain extracellular vesicle (EV) proteomics to identify protein responses to acute neuroinflammation and an EV-based microRNA intervention. Rats received vehicle, intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or LPS followed by an intravenous EV formulation containing anti-inflammatory microRNAs (miRNAs). Brains were collected 24 h after LPS or vehicle administration, and three independently processed animal-derived EV-enriched preparations per group were analyzed by label-free proteomics. Across all nine samples, 953 protein groups had complete normalized abundance measurements. Compared with vehicle controls, LPS exposure was associated with 227 exploratory protein changes, comprising 95 increases and 132 decreases at nominal P < 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change >= log2(1.5). Increased proteins were enriched for translation-related annotations, whereas decreased proteins were enriched for plasma-membrane annotations. These LPS-associated changes did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of q < 0.05. Following treatment, 119 of the 227 candidates were closer to control abundance on the log2 scale; 23 candidates also showed nominal treatment-versus-LPS differences. Lamb2 and Ptgfrn were the two proteins that differed significantly between treated and LPS-only animals after FDR correction, identifying them as priorities for further validation. Nevertheless, 174 proteins differed significantly between treated animals and vehicle controls, and analysis across the measured proteins did not demonstrate an overall shift toward control values. Thus, the intervention was associated with specific protein responses, but treated animals retained substantial differences from controls. This study identifies candidate markers for investigating treatment responses in brain EV-enriched preparations and demonstrates the value of examining individual proteins alongside broader proteomic changes. Independent validation is needed to determine their functional relevance and distinguish miRNA-specific effects from contributions of the administered EV carrier.

title: Intrastriatal injection of amplified Lewy body dementia (LBD) fibrils in mice results in accumulation of fibrils with LBD structure and neurodegeneration
abstract: The defining neuropathologic feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) is alpha-synuclein (Asyn) fibril accumulation in Lewy bodies (LBs) and Lewy neurites (LNs). Recently, we developed a method to amplify Asyn fibrils derived from human post-mortem LBD brain tissue and determined that the structure of amplified Asyn fibrils is highly similar to the structure of fibrils directly isolated from LBD brain tissue. We examined whether injection of these fibrils into humanized Asyn mice recapitulates pathologic Asyn fibril accumulation with human LBD Asyn fibril structure. We utilized mice containing a null allele in the mouse Snca gene and a human SNCA transgene. Intrastriatal injection of amplified Asyn fibrils derived from 3 different LBD autopsy cases resulted in cytoplasmic and neuritic phospho-Asyn accumulation in the striatum, cortex, and amygdala bilaterally at 3mpi. Fibril injections produced a reduction in the number of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with LB-like inclusions in surviving neurons, and produced impaired sensorimotor function as measured on the accelerating rotarod test. Fibril accumulation increased 3.6-fold between 1 and 3 months post-injection (mpi) and was relatively stable between 3 and 5 mpi. We amplified fibrils from mouse brain tissue 5 mpi and collected single-particle cryo-EM data. High resolution 3D structural information could not be obtained because of the lack of helical twist, but comparison of the cryo-EM 2D class averages with those derived from amplified fibrils prepared from human LBD tissue revealed multiple matching classes, indicating that the Lewy fold is maintained in the fibrils that accumulate in mouse brain tissue. Our findings demonstrate an approach to model the accumulation of Asyn fibrils with LBD structure in mice, providing a platform for investigating disease mechanisms, imaging biomarkers, and therapeutics targeting Asyn in PD/LBD.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology and Hope Center for Neurological Disorders, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO, 63110, USA

title: Hyperglycaemia reversibly disrupts circadian behaviour in mice
abstract: Disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms are among the most common features of diabetes, and are known to raise the risk of developing the disease. Whether the relationship also runs the other way, with diabetes itself disrupting the clock, has remained unresolved. Using an inducible mouse model of diabetes, in which hyperglycaemia can be induced and then reversed within the same animal, we show that elevated blood glucose is a reversible cause of circadian disruption. Raising blood glucose reduced the amplitude of circadian rest-activity rhythms by 50%, in proportion to the degree of hyperglycaemia, and shortened the free-running period of the clock. Restoring normoglycaemia reversed both effects. Diabetic animals had a delayed phase of activity onset, i.e. later chronotype, and re-entrained more slowly after a simulated jet lag. However, phase shifting to nocturnal light pulses was intact, suggesting normal photic responses. Brain glucose and O-GlcNAcylation, a nutrient-sensitive protein modification, were both elevated in diabetic animals, showing that peripheral hyperglycaemia reaches the brain and alters its metabolic state, and providing a molecular readout of that exposure. Together, these findings establish that a peripheral metabolic state is a reversible determinant of circadian rest-activity behaviour, completing a bidirectional link between blood glucose and the clock and arguing that the two must be treated together rather than in isolation.

title: Integration of Neuroimaging and Histopathology in a Squirrel Monkey Model of Spontaneous Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy and Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities
abstract: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a prevalent cerebrovascular pathology in AD and contributes to amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), a major complication of current anti-amyloid immunotherapy. Despite its growing clinical importance, critical gaps remain in the development of reliable biomarkers for antemortem diagnosis of CAA. Squirrel monkeys (SQMs) are a valuable non-human primate model with translational relevance due to their universal propensity to develop abundant CAA and spontaneous ARIA in geriatric animals. The present study employed R2*, the apparent transverse relaxation rate, which is sensitive to susceptibility-related tissue properties, including iron content and blood oxygenation levels, to monitor age-related brain pathology in SQMs with varying CAA severity. Young, early geriatric, and late geriatric SQMs underwent 7T MRI using a dual-purpose T2*-w 3D multi-gradient-echo sequence for high-resolution anatomy and quantitative R2* mapping, alongside T2-w/FLAIR imaging. Whole-brain and gray matter R2* increased with age. In contrast, white matter R2* showed an initial increase followed by a late-life reversal, likely reflecting age-related changes in myelin integrity, tissue microstructure, and tissue water content. MRI-histopathology correlation linked T2*-w MRI hypointensities to CAA-positive iron-laden vessels associated with perivascular inflammation and, in some cases, hemosiderin deposits. Here we confirmed the occurrence of ARIA-H and ARIA-E events in geriatric animals. SQMs provided a valuable opportunity to examine the underlying pathology of spontaneous ARIA-E, revealing distinctive tissue signatures associated with its manifestation. ARIA-E hyperintensities were characterized by reactive gliosis and BBB disruption, whereas more advanced lesions exhibited perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and evidence of myelin and axonal injury. The current study presents compelling evidence linking R2* alterations with CAA severity and ARIA-related tissue injury, providing a foundation for further advancing early detection of CAA, ARIA risk assessment, and treatment strategies.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, New York University Grossman School of Medicine, New York, NY, USA

title: Sleep-dependent modulation of thalamic brain temperature estimates in humans
abstract: Mammalian thermal physiology is geared towards dissipating heat during sleep. Brain temperature typically decreases during non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep in all mammalian species measured to date, yet non-invasive confirmation in healthy humans is lacking: the only available human study used invasive recordings in epileptic patients without a wake control condition. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) enables brain temperature mapping non-invasively, using the temperature-sensitive chemical shift of water relative to N-Acetyl-Aspartate as an internal reference. First, we validated that with metabolite cycling (MC), a MRS approach that enables the simultaneous acquisition of metabolite and water information without conventional water suppression, can be used to determine estimates of brain temperature in an ex vivo sheep head. Next, we determined that by using a temporal resolution of ~4 minutes, we obtained high-quality spectra without losing excessive temporal resolution. We then re-analyzed an existing set of MRS data (acquired with the MC sequence) of the thalamus in young adults (n=9) who slept in the evening for up to 2 hours in the scanner, to assess sleep-evoked changes in estimates of brain temperature. Of the nine participants, five participants took part in the subsequent wake-only experiment, allowing to control for the potential impact of circadian time and body posture on estimates of brain temperature. Sleep-wake states were quantified with standard polysomnography, confirming that the participants managed to sleep in the scanner. On average, they spent 39.4+/-15.7 min in N2 sleep, 24.8+/-18.1 min in N3 sleep, 10.0+/-4.9 min in N1 sleep, and 37.0+/-19.6 min awake. Estimates of brain temperature were correlated across the sleep and wake-only experiment within the same participant (R^2=0.29, P<0.0001). When participants entered NREM sleep, estimates of brain temperature decreased by 0.2 degrees Celcius. Moreover, the deeper NREM sleep, the more pronounced the decrease in estimates of brain temperature (P=0.014). These data suggest that an evening nap consisting of NREM sleep decreases thalamic temperature. Considering the profound impact temperature can have on brain functioning, these brain temperature changes could be a pathway through which sleep impacts the brain.

title: Deciphering auditory neuroprogenitor stemness for large-scale neuronal screening
abstract: Sensorineural hearing loss can arise from damage to sensory hair cells, auditory neurons or their synaptic connections, with auditory neuropathy and cochlear synaptopathy highlighting the importance of neural integrity for hearing. The mammalian cochlea has limited capacity to regenerate lost auditory neurons. Understanding the molecular programs that sustain cochlear progenitor expansion and neurogenic competence could support neuronal regeneration and provide renewable models for auditory drug discovery. We previously established that WNT activation combined with dual SMAD inhibition (CHIR-DS) supports scalable expansion and neuronal differentiation of mouse auditory neuroprogenitors (ANPGs). Here, we characterize the transcriptional, chromatin and metabolic changes associated with the induced state. RNA-seq and ATAC-seq identified reduced Id1 and Id2 expression and increased accessibility at proneural basic helix-loop-helix motifs, alongside transcriptional enrichment of translation, mTOR and glucose-metabolism programs. Compared with growth-factor controls, CHIR-DS-treated ANPGs showed slight increase in glycolysis at early passage. However, after long-term expansion, both glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were markedly enhanced. Human fetal ANPGs also responded to CHIR-DS with increased sphere growth and retained neural differentiation capacity, providing proof of concept beyond the mouse system. Finally, neurons derived from stemness-induced ANPGs (siANs) supported a 384-well reporter assay and a 2,560-compound pilot screen that nominated candidate neurite-outgrowth enhancers. Together, these findings validate the pathway basis of ANPG stemness induction, characterize the resulting molecular and metabolic state, and demonstrate human feasibility and a neuronal screening application.
author_corresponding_institution: The inner ear and Olfaction lab, Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland

title: Criticality-related dynamics accompany long-term functional decline in primary cortical MEA cultures
abstract: Primary cortical neuron cultures are widely used to study network development and decline, but their long-term electrophysiological trajectories are poorly characterized. We used multi-electrode arrays to longitudinally monitor Wistar rat cortical cultures for up to ~730 days in vitro (DIV), combining activity measures with survival analysis and criticality metrics. Wells shared an early developmental phase, with mean firing rate peaking at 12-14 Hz around DIV 100-150, before diverging into two phenotypes: early-death wells, showing progressive loss of burst organization, longer inter-burst intervals, shorter bursts, and steep declines in active-electrode recruitment; and long-survival wells, which sustained organized bursting and measurable activity well beyond DIV 400, in some cases past DIV 700. Cox proportional-hazards modeling with FDR correction across thirteen candidate features identified burst duration, inter-burst interval, synchrony, mean firing rate, branching ratio, and Kappa index as significant predictors of time to network failure. Criticality metrics offered the most mechanistic insight: in early-death wells, branching ratio declined toward zero and Kappa index rose toward its upper bound as networks approached silencing. Beyond their average levels, the rate of change of branching ratio and Kappa index over recordings was the strongest correlate of survival time among all criticality metrics. Neuronal avalanche size and duration exponents and their scaling relation, remained consistent with scale-free dynamics in both phenotypes while networks were active, though avalanche occurrence rate declined progressively in early-death wells without reaching significance as an independent predictor. These results show that long-term network survival is not determined by firing rate alone, but by preserved burst organization, sustained electrode recruitment and near-critical propagation dynamics. This work offers one of the longest electrophysiological characterizations of rodent cortical cultures to date and identifies criticality-based metrics as promising tools for predicting network decline and evaluating interventions to preserve long-term neuronal function.

title: Scan field rotation with a K-mirror for fast two-photon imaging along curved planes
abstract: In contrast to the curved geometry of biological structures, the imaging plane of conventional microscopes is flat. In principle, axial scanning can adjust the focus to follow curved structures. In resonant scanning microscopes, which are broadly used for video-rate functional imaging, however, such focus adjustment is typically possible at rates faster than the slow (~30 Hz) scan axis but not as fast as the fast (~8000 Hz) resonant axis. The fixed direction of the fast resonant axis therefore constrains how the imaging plane can be tilted or curved using axial scanning, and limits how well it can be aligned with biological structures of interest. Here, we present an optical modification that overcomes this constraint. Specifically, we combine scan field rotation using a K-mirror with fast axial scanning using an electrically tunable lens. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach for calcium imaging by aligning the imaging plane with the curved pyramidal cell layer in mouse hippocampus, increasing the number of simultaneously imaged neurons. In addition, we image dendritic arbors of hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons that would otherwise be only partially accessible for fast imaging, and we apply our method to the curved layers of cerebellar Purkinje cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate how scan field rotation can be used to optimally orient a dendritic branch for high-speed subcellular glutamate imaging. Our approach is based on a single module and can therefore be retrofitted to standard two-photon systems. We openly share design specifications, 3D-printed parts, and custom ScanImage-compatible code to facilitate rapid adoption.

title: A hippocampal digital Twin reveals latent structure in freely flying bats
abstract: Concurrent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), large-scale neuronal recording, and behavioral tracking have enabled increasingly powerful predictive models of brain-behavior relationships. Yet predictive accuracy does not automatically yield interpretable principles of neural organization, particularly during natural behavior, where the relevant variables computed are often unknown in advance. Here, we developed a functional digital twin of the hippocampus, trained jointly on large-scale neural activity and self-directed three-dimensional flight in freely flying bats. A multimodal, multitask transformer accurately predicted both neural activity and behavior, outperformed standard approaches, and generalized across recording sessions. Interrogating the model's representations suggested a form of hippocampal generalization across self-selected trajectories that was not apparent in physical coordinates, but was plainly visible in the model's low-dimensional latent space. We confirmed this organization directly in the recorded neural activity: neurons fired at corresponding stages of spatially distinct paths connecting the same origin and destination, preserving their relative firing order even as their firing fields shifted with the path. Analysis of neuron-specific readouts further identified functional relationships among neurons that generalized from flight to waking rest and sleep, brain states never used for training, and differed systematically between the hippocampal subregions CA1 and CA3. Together, these results show how AI-based functional digital twins can complement conventional analysis by generating testable hypotheses about neural organization during natural behavior.

title: A foundation model for brain organoid network dynamics uncovers intrinsic computation and convergent disease phenotypes
abstract: Brain organoids develop self-organizing neural networks that can be used to model neurodevelopment and disease. Here we introduce PULSE, a foundation model developed using over 900 hours of high-density microelectrode array recordings of in vitro and ex vivo neural tissue. We show that this single model can address two open questions: how disease-associated variants alter network development, and how naive circuits encode information. PULSE revealed accelerated network maturation in held-out human 16p11.2-deletion organoids. It also revealed a change in network coordination shared with SHANK3 deficiency. Because organoids develop without sensory input, they let us ask how circuits encode information before any representation is learned. Closed-loop control of a virtual inverted pendulum engaged existing spontaneous activity patterns rather than creating new ones. PULSE provides a common reference frame for neural circuits across genotypes, protocols and tasks.

title: A Control-Theoretic Account of Cognitive Effort in Working Memory
abstract: Cognitive effort is closely linked to prefrontal control, but the control demands imposed by working memory remain poorly understood at the level of neural circuits. We formulated frontoparietal regulation as a feedback-control problem in a conductance-based spiking network comprising an intraparietal ring attractor and a recurrent dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) actuator. A local data-driven task-actuator model was identified around the cue-offset mnemonic state and used to design linear-quadratic regulation. Increasing memory load produced a strong monotonic rise in realized post-cue control effort, driven primarily by sustained dlPFC recruitment. Cue-aligned selective routing supported higher mnemonic loads with substantially less control effort than spatially nonspecific routing. Mean-matched open-loop stimulation reproduced much of the nominal retention benefit, whereas state-dependent feedback provided greater robustness when mnemonic activity was perturbed. Finite-horizon analysis revealed a strongly anisotropic, effectively low-dimensional control geometry dominated by a common mnemonic direction, with much weaker access to item-differentiating directions. These results link increasing working-memory demand to greater sustained prefrontal control requirements and show how frontoparietal routing geometry shapes the efficiency and robustness of mnemonic regulation.

title: Lysosomal Glycosaminoglycan Catabolism Regulates Microglial Cell State in the Developing CNS
abstract: Remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM), a complex structural and signaling network of the nervous system, is essential for CNS development, plasticity, and injury responses, yet how individual neural cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that phagocytic clearance of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major components of the ECM, is an intrinsic function of microglia in the developing CNS. Our studies reveal an unexpected finding that impaired GAG clearance shifts microglia toward a non-homeostatic cell state seen in immature and disease-associated microglia (DAM), supporting a reciprocal relationship between the ECM and microglia. Using mouse models of Mucopolysaccharidosis VII, we examined the consequences of deleting {beta}-glucuronidase (GUSB), a lysosomal enzyme required for GAG degradation. Loss of GUSB causes early accumulation of undegraded chondroitin sulfate within microglial lysosomes, as confirmed by LC-MS analysis of intracellular GAGs isolated from cortical microglia. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified Gusb-null microglia as a distinct transcriptional population enriched for a core transcriptome shared by immature and disease-associated microglia. Together, these findings establish lysosomal GAG catabolism as a pathway that links ECM remodeling to the acquisition of adult homeostatic microglial identity during CNS development.

title: Progranulin deficiency promotes neuroinflammation through cathepsin B-mediated activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome
abstract: Haploinsufficiency of progranulin (resulting from mutations in the GRN gene) is a major genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD), which is characterized by profound changes in personality and behavior, progressive impairments in executive function, speech, language and/or movement, TDP-43 pathology, lysosomal dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Studies in progranulin-deficient mouse models have demonstrated the critical role of neuroinflammation in disease pathogenesis, as deletion of NF-kB or complement factors prevents FTD-associated behavioral deficits. While progranulin is known to be anti-inflammatory, the precise molecular mechanism by which its deficiency triggers inflammatory cascades remain unclear. Here, we investigate the involvement of the NLRP3 inflammasome in progranulin-deficient models, including mice, human microglial cells, and patient fibroblasts. In Grn mice, we found increased levels of several inflammasome-related proteins, including procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Similarly, GRN knockout (KO) microglia cells showed significant increases in levels of procaspase-1, NLRP3, and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Moreover, KO cells had increased NLRP3 oligomerization, suggesting that progranulin negatively regulates inflammasome assembly. We also investigated the potential link between lysosomal dysfunction and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in progranulin deficiency. We found that pharmacological inhibition of cathepsin B reduced NLRP3 inflammasome oligomerization as well as inflammatory cytokine expression in GRN KO cells. Additionally, siRNA knockdown of cathepsin B reduced levels of procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} in GRN KO cells. Finally, we found that heterozygous GRN fibroblasts exhibited similar increases in procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} levels, and these increases were corrected by treatment with an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that increase progranulin protein levels. Overall, our results demonstrate that progranulin deficiency promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activity through cathepsin B-mediated signaling, thereby establishing a mechanistic link between lysosomal dysfunction and increased inflammation. The ability of the GRN-targeting ASO to correct NLRP3-mediated inflammation highlights a promising therapeutic strategy for FTD-GRN and inflammation in other neurodegenerative disorders linked to progranulin deficiency.
author_corresponding_institution: Saint Louis University School of Medicine

title: Clustering of the Adhesion-GPCR Latrophilin-3 Drives Excitatory Synapse Assembly
abstract: Precise control of synapse formation is essential for brain function. Adhesion-GPCRs combine adhesion, signaling, and scaffold recruitment to regulate synapse formation, yet their mechanisms of action remain unclear. Here, we identify nanoscale clustering of the adhesion-GPCR Latrophilin-3 as a key mechanism regulating excitatory synapse assembly. We find that endogenous Latrophilin-3 forms densely packed nanoclusters, with larger nanoclusters enriched at excitatory synapses. To probe the functional significance of Latrophilin-3 clustering, we engineered an optogenetically controlled Latrophilin-3. Light-induced Latrophilin-3 clustering triggered robust excitatory synapse formation, which required both Latrophilin-3-mediated G-protein signaling and postsynaptic scaffold recruitment. Strikingly, clustering of a mutant Latrophilin-3 lacking known ligand-binding domains still promoted synapse formation, indicating that Latrophilin-3 ligands induce synapse assembly primarily by clustering Latrophilin-3. Our findings suggest a general paradigm by which extracellular ligand-induced clustering activates adhesion-GPCRs by generating compartmentalized signaling, which in the case of Latrophilin-3, cooperates with postsynaptic scaffold recruitment to drive synapse assembly.

title: Arousal-informed neuronal avalanches operate near criticality
abstract: Cortical networks are thought to operate near a "critical point" that optimizes information processing, but this has been difficult to test at single-cell resolution across large brain areas, as narrow fields of view miss overlapping neural avalanches, causing subcritical estimates, Using mesoscopic two-photon calcium imaging in awake mouse visual cortex, we recorded thousands of neurons and applied convolutional non-negative matrix factorization to decompose population activity into distinct, overlapping spatiotemporal avalanches. Rather than occupying a single dynamical state, we find that the cortex hosts multiple overlapping subnetworks distributed across a phase diagram at varying distances from the critical point. Arousal-linked avalanches propagate widely and operate nearest the critical point, showing optimized dynamic range, minimized algorithmic complexity, and maximized temporal entropy. Our results reveal how the awake brain tunes parallel near-critical subnetworks to support robust sensory computation.

title: The Neural Protective Effects of Intermittent Fasting in Adult Drosophila Following Traumatic Brain Injury Exposure.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of neurological-based morbidity and mortality in different human populations. Repetitive, mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is increasingly recognized as a contributor to progressive neural attrition. Dietary measures that are neural protective could provide an accessible means for impacted human populations to alter outcomes in relation to neurological diseases. Intermittent fasting (IF) has been associated with metabolic and neuroprotective benefits for several neurological disease models, including Drosophila melanogaster models that are used to study neurological disorders linked to TBI exposure. Using two IF regimens, we examined the outcomes of adult Drosophila in conjunction with aging and mTBI. Overall, when exposed to trauma, IF-treated adult cohorts exhibited longer lifespans, lower mortality rates and improved behavioral responses. This included young (10-day) and middle aged (21-day) flies exposed to either Pre- or Post-IF conditions. Additionally, expression analysis showed IF treatments significantly reduced expression levels of Drosophila inflammatory markers (AMPs) in adult neural tissues from traumatized flies. The indications are that the net positive impact of IF found for longevity and trauma responses could be due to lower levels of secondary neuronal damage.

title: Neurite Complexity and Plasticity Markers Track Synaptic Vesicle Density in the Living Human Brain: A Multimodal PET-MRI-EEG Study
abstract: Neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganise its structure and function, is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases and a putative mechanism of action for pharmacological interventions. [11C]-UCBJ positron emission tomography (PET), which quantifies synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) density, offers the most direct in vivo measure of human synaptic density, but its relationship to complementary, more scalable neuroimaging measures of structural and functional plasticity remains uncharacterised. We combined [11C]-UCBJ PET, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI/NODDI), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG)-based sensory tasks (roving mismatch negativity, MMN; visual long-term potentiation, vLTP) in 18 healthy volunteers to test the relationship between synaptic terminal SV2A density and complementary structural and functional neuroplasticity measures, and whether these relationships were reproducible following pharmacological challenge with ketamine (n = 11) or N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT; n = 7). There were no statistically significant differences in PET-derived SV2A binding potential (BPND), DWI-derived neurite orientation dispersion (ODI) and structural weighted degree (SWD), EEG-derived MMN repetition suppression, and late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation, 1 to 8 days following DMT and ketamine exposure compared to baseline. BPND was coupled with ODI across cortical regions before and after pharmacological challenge, and this relationship was tighter within visual, attentional, and frontoparietal control brain networks. SWD showed a weaker, more spatially restricted association with BPND, primarily in regions belonging to the limbic and visual brain networks, but was not replicated post-drug. No consistent association was found between BPND and functional weighted degree (FWD), derived from rs-fMRI, at baseline or after pharmacological challenge. Frontotemporal BPND was positively associated with MMN repetition suppression (r = 0.61), and occipital BPND with late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation (r = 0.54), with the MMN-BPND association replicating after pharmacological challenge (r = 0.49). These findings link synaptic terminal SV2A density in the living human brain to neurite architecture and the capacity for short-term and Hebbian-like long-term synaptic plasticity, while dissociating these relationships from generic functional connectivity and magnitude of sensory-evoked responses. These data provide cross-modal validation for DWI- and EEG-derived measures as biological indices and surrogate measures of human synaptic plasticity.

title: High-throughput light-sheet 3D microscopy of whole rodent brain microstructure for integration with MRI
abstract: Whole-brain cellular mapping is essential for understanding how differences in cellular architecture shape brain organisation and function. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides whole-brain coverage in humans and animal models but is only indirectly sensitive to cellular features. Integrating MRI with whole-brain microscopy is therefore critical for interpreting existing microstructural MRI metrics and developing new, more specific ones. Here, we present a scalable cross-resolution framework that integrates 3D light-sheet microscopy (LSM) of intact rodent brains with diffusion MRI (dMRI) to bridge cellular and macroscopic brain imaging. By combining active electrotransport-based tissue clearing and immunolabelling with accelerated LSM acquisitions, we achieve whole-brain multiplexed mapping of neuronal and glial populations in intact rodent brains on timescales comparable to conventional histology and 2D microscopy. This throughput enables LSM and MRI integration at scale, linking macroscopic MRI contrasts to microscopic cellular features within the same tissue. We apply this framework across eight genetically diverse mouse strains to develop predictive models of 3D microscopy-derived cellular features from multi-shell dMRI-derived contrasts. We demonstrate that data-driven combinations of state-of-the-art dMRI contrasts predict neuronal and astrocytic features better than individual contrasts, across all animals. Our novel approach enables 3D microscopy to guide the development and interpretation of microstructural MRI measures that are ultimately translatable to the living human brain.
author_corresponding_institution: Sir Peter Mansfield Imaging Centre, School of Medicine, University of Nottingham

title: Neuronal FICD shapes motivated behavior through modulation of dopamine receptor dynamics
abstract: Motivated behaviors rely on dopaminergic signaling, which in turn depends on the correct folding and trafficking of receptors through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Within the ER, the AMPylase enzyme FICD acts as a molecular rheostat through its modification of the chaperone BiP, dynamically tuning the organelle's responsiveness to folding perturbations and cellular stress. While the biochemistry of FICD is well-established, its role in complex animal behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FICD as a conserved contributor to the generation of motivated behavior. In Drosophila, pan-neuronal knockdown of dFic significantly reduces feeding, spontaneous locomotion, and reward-seeking behavior. These alterations occur without disrupting circadian architecture, motor capacity, or homeostatic hunger, indicating a specific loss of motivational drive. Depleting dFic within subsets of dopamine receptor-expressing (Dop1R1) neurons recapitulates these behavioral alterations. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that dFic depletion does not induce a canonical unfolded protein response, pointing to a specific post-transcriptional alteration rather than global ER stress. At the molecular level, dysregulated dFic alters the localization and abundance of Dop1R1. Finally, we demonstrate that this regulatory axis is evolutionarily conserved, as loss of FICD similarly diminishes motivated behaviors in C. elegans and mice. Together, these findings implicate FICD in the generation of motivated behavior and link dynamic control of ER proteostasis to dopamine-receptor maturation.

title: A Multiverse Approach to Brain Age Prediction: Exploring the Impact of Modality, Bias Adjustment, and Atlas
abstract: Brain age, an individual's age predicted from neuroimaging data, is a promising biomarker of brain health. Yet brain age estimates may depend on methodological choices within the prediction pipeline. We used a multiverse approach to systematically investigate effects of data modality, bias-adjustment method, and brain parcellation on brain-age prediction using data from 560 healthy adults (18.6-89 years) from the CamCAN dataset. Across 84 pipeline conditions, chronological age was predicted from connectivity features with elastic net regression, and performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE). A multilevel model tested the effects of the pipeline factors and their interactions; moreover, cross-atlas consistency of the most predictive connections was assessed. MAEs varied substantially across conditions (5.26-18.30 years). Modality and bias adjustment had significant effects on MAE and interacted significantly. Concatenating structural and functional connectivity performed similarly to structural connectivity alone, and structure-function coupling produced the highest MAE in most conditions. Beheshti-based bias adjustment outperformed Cole-based adjustment, while combining adjustment procedures did not consistently improve performance. Atlas choice had no main effect on MAE, its interaction with modality was significant but negligible in size, and finer parcellations did not systematically improve performance. However, the network-level features driving predictions showed limited spatial overlap across atlases, and importance was distributed over many features. Brain-age prediction is thus sensitive to methodological choices, particularly modality and bias-adjustment strategy. Atlas choice appears less important for predictive accuracy but may affect which connections appear most predictive. These findings highlight the importance of systematically evaluating analytical choices in brain-age research.

title: Reuse of learned subtask representations during human planning
abstract: The notion of a compositional reuse of previously learned problem solutions predicts that the human brain should reinstate such learned subtask representations during planning. Here, we test this in a value-ranking task implemented in an online and a magnetoencephalography (MEG) experiment, respectively. Participants first learned pairwise rankings and subsequently solved problems where these learned rankings could either be reused or required reordering. Behaviourally, in the online experiment, we show the availability of a reusable subtask structure improved accuracy, with computational modelling indicating a greater weighting of subtask-level value when participants could avail of this learnt structure. In MEG, during planning, we show enhanced reactivation of task-relevant subtask representations in the reusable condition, and particularly so early in the experiment. In a subsequent probe task, we show subtask-identity representations generalised to a novel context and that stimuli belonging to the same learned subtask manifest an increase in their neural similarity. Temporally delayed linear modelling (TDLM) revealed forward and backward sequential reactivation at a subtask level, alongside backward stimulus-level replay, with subtask sequenceness varying according to task context. The findings provide convergent behavioural, computational and neural evidence for reactivation and reuse of learnt relational structures for novel problem solving.
author_corresponding_institution: Max Planck UCL Centre for Computational Psychiatry and Ageing Research, University College London, UK

title: Thoughts and cortical responses are shaped by the type of change at event boundaries
abstract: Continuous experience is divided into discrete and meaningful events, but different kinds of event transitions may shape thought and brain activity in different ways. We examined how perceived event boundaries relate to visual, auditory, and semantic features, ongoing thought, and large-scale cortical states during movie-watching. We combined three independent samples who viewed the same eight movie clips, aligning these measures to a shared stimulus timeline: One marked event boundaries, one reported ongoing thought, and one was scanned with fMRI. Whole-brain spatial correlations showed that event boundaries correlated positively with visual change and negatively with auditory change, but not with any thought pattern. Time-resolved analyses showed that boundaries were associated with a reduction in distracted thoughts and brain states positioned toward visual processing. Clustering boundaries by movie feature change profile identified visual, semantic, interruption, and narrative boundary types. All four types showed a shift toward visual processing in the brain, but their other associations differed. Visual boundaries were associated with less distraction, semantic boundaries with thoughts related to past experience and prior knowledge, and narrative boundaries with more detailed and deliberate thoughts. Visual and semantic boundaries also showed distinct shifts in brain state that were not apparent in the other two types. These findings suggest that event boundaries mark a set of state shifts in ongoing experience, with a shared reorientation toward visual processing and changes in thought and brain state that vary with the type of transition.

title: Oligodendrocyte stress response as a driver of vascular dementia
abstract: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a prevalent and devastating neurocognitive disorder characterized by profound white matter damage, yet the precise cellular mechanisms linking cerebrovascular stress to demyelination remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize the impact of a chronic cardiometabolic stress regimen combining a high-fat diet and hypertension (HF/HBP) on central nervous system structure and function. Adult HF/HBP mice exhibit progressive oligodendroglial cell loss and myelin thinning, followed by cognitive impairments, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits that recapitulate clinical features of VaD. Mechanistically, we identify the integrated stress response (ISR) as a central driver of this pathology; pharmacological inhibition of the ISR restores myelination, while cell-specific genetic deletion of the ISR-activating kinase PERK from oligodendrocytes fully protects mice from HF/HBP-induced pathological and behavioral defects. Furthermore, we provide translational evidence that the ISR is activated in oligodendrocytes in human cases of cerebrovascular disease. Together, these findings reveal a critical, cell-autonomous role for oligodendroglial ISR activation during cerebrovascular stress and position this pathway as a viable therapeutic target to mitigate VaD pathogenesis.

title: Exploring the role of multivariate associations between brain networks and gut microbiota in (food) value-based decision-making
abstract: Food reward valuation and decision making are key psychological processes regulating eating behaviour. Stress and negative affect can shape these processes, increasing vulnerability to overeating high caloric, ultra-processed foods and thereby elevating obesity risk. Yet not all individuals under stress exhibit such behavioural shifts, highlighting the need to understand which modulating factors explain this inter individual variability. Emerging evidence suggests that anxiety-/stress-induced changes in gut microbiota might alter reward sensitivity via the gut-brain axis. An integrative framework linking microbiota, neural, and affective processes is thus essential for explaining individual differences in emotional eating, yet such a framework is still lacking. To this end, supervised linked independent component analysis (Super- BigFLICA) was used to explore multivariate gut-brain latent components guided by affective and body composition indexes in healthy participants (N = 592) from the Healthy Brain Study. Next, general linear models were used to identify if any of the observed components were predictive of elevated unhealthy food valuation and choice in a food auction task. A multimodal component was predictive of both food valuation and choice. This component was characterized by co-occurring changes in several gut bacterial taxa at the genus level (e.g., UCG-010 and DTU089), specific connectivity between reward-related brain regions (e.g., nucleus accumbens, caudate), and was clearly linked to elevated anxiety sensitivity, life-event impact, and body mass index. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of supervised gut-brain integration for predicting behaviour and reveal a potential phenotype linking microbiota composition, brain function, and emotional state that should be further investigated
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Medical Neuroscience, Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, The Netherlands

title: Linking anterior cingulate sulcal variability to attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder behavior
abstract: Background: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is consistently implicated in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ACC variability, including its most variable structure, the paracingulate sulcus (PCGS), has been known since the late 1800s, and since then, has been linked to cognitive control, impulsivity, and psychiatric conditions comorbid with ADHD, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Yet, the role of the PCGS in ADHD remains unexamined at the individual level. Methods: We characterized PCGS incidence, asymmetry, and morphology in 247 children and adolescents (144 ADHD: 10.9 +/- 2.73 years old, 75% male; 103 neurotypical: 12.2 +/- 3.17 years old, 50% male) from the ADHD-200 dataset. The PCGS was manually identified in FreeSurfer cortical surface reconstructions. Morphometric measures, including sulcal length, depth, and cortical thickness, were extracted and normalized to hemisphere-wide variables. Between-group analyses tested whether PCGS presence, asymmetry, and quantitative morphology differed by diagnosis, while behavioral analyses examined associations with inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and cognitive measures. Age and gender were included as covariates. Results: Analyses revealed that, in both NT and ADHD individuals, there was significant leftward asymmetry in PCGS presence. Between groups, the PCGS was less likely to be present in individuals with ADHD in the left hemisphere. Leftward PCGS absence was also associated with significantly higher ADHD index and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores. Conclusions: These findings advance understanding of how early neurodevelopmental variation in cortical folding may serve as a structural intermediary between genetic liability and the behavioral expression of ADHD.

title: Adaptive co-transmission shapes sensory encoding and behavior
abstract: Co-transmission expands the chemical repertoire of neurons, but whether coexisting neurotransmitters can be independently organized and remodeled by experience to control distinct aspects of behavior remains unclear. Here, we address this question in the AFD thermosensory neuron of Caenorhabditis elegans, which directs navigation toward a learned temperature preference. We find that glutamatergic and cholinergic vesicular transporters coexist within individual presynaptic boutons but differ in axonal trafficking, subsynaptic organization, and dependence on presynaptic machinery. Sensory experience differentially regulates the two systems: animals trained to prefer higher temperatures exhibit increased VGLUT/EAT-4 abundance, whereas those trained to prefer lower temperatures exhibit increased VAChT/UNC-17 abundance. The two transmitters also make distinct, context-dependent contributions to goal-directed navigation. Glutamatergic transmission promotes movement toward the learned thermal preference, whereas cholinergic transmission restrains continued migration beyond it. Analysis of locomotor trajectories further reveals that the two transmitters differentially regulate reorientation decisions across regions of the thermal gradient. Together, these findings identify adaptive co-transmission, a form of synaptic plasticity in which coexisting neurotransmitter systems are differentially organized and regulated by experience, and make distinct, context-dependent contributions to behavior.

title: Hebbian learning generates individuality in spatial decision-making
abstract: Individuals exposed to similar environments often develop consistent behavioral differences, yet how learning generates individuality remains unclear. We study agents whose neural connections develop through unsupervised Hebbian learning during pursuit of a moving target. All agents begin with identical networks without recurrent connections and neurons tuned to world-fixed directions. The target coactivates neurons with overlapping directional receptive fields while leaving more distant neurons relatively inactive. Hebbian learning converts this activity pattern into local excitation and longer-range inhibition. Stochastic differences in target motion and neural activity during learning produce individual-specific departures from each network's average center-surround profile. We then freeze the connections and repeatedly test agents with two equally attractive targets, a task absent from training. Individual agents tend to spend more time near one target than the other, with preferences differing among agents but remaining repeatable across trials.
