title: Sense-Making phase transition framework for Affect
abstract: Contemporary accounts of affect emphasize different perspectives, ranging from the regulation of bodily states in allostatic approaches to the relational and sense-making character stressed by enactive theories. Here, we show that affect can be made explicit within the sense-making phase transition framework previously introduced for the perception of an inner sensation. Within this same formal structure, each stable minimum of the sense-making potential defines an affective state: its position determines valence, while its depth determines arousal. Affect therefore is not introduced as an independent ingredient, but emerges as the associated state in the valence-arousal space, providing a link between allostatic and enactive approaches to affect. This formulation distinguishes valence intensity from arousal, allows for dominant and secondary affective states, and naturally accommodates mixed-valence configurations beyond a strictly bipolar description. Revisiting representative landscapes of the model, we show how neutral, uncertain, polarized, and mixed-valence regimes arise as a function of contextual sensory information, learned historical evaluation, and externally supplied information. We further show that the resulting valence-arousal relation provides a theoretical basis for the upper-open V-shaped organization discussed in the affect literature, while also opening a natural route toward a dynamical description of affect and emotions.

title: Rewiring of adult neural networks - learning from structural plasticity across multiple scales
abstract: Synaptic connections are continuously formed and eliminated even in adult neuronal networks. This process - called structural plasticity - allows networks to change their topology to learn and adapt to their environment or compensate for lesions. Yet, in contrast to synaptic plasticity, structural plasticity is less well studied and understood. We here present the current state of knowledge as well as open problems in the field along three guiding questions: (1) What regulates structural plasticity in biological neural networks? (2) What are the functional consequences and advantages of structural plasticity in adult neural networks? (3) How can our understanding of structural plasticity be translated into clinical and technological applications? We argue that understanding structural plasticity is a problem involving multiple temporal and spatial scales. Solving this problem thus requires collaborative efforts of experimentalists, theoreticians as well as computational modelers, and has the potential for comprehensive neuroscientific insights that can guide the development of medical applications, artificial neural networks as well as neuromorphic computing.

title: Rethinking World Models for Biosignals
abstract: World models promise to learn how systems evolve and respond to actions, enabling simulation, planning and decision-making. Bringing this promise to biosignals requires more than accurate prediction of physiological recordings. We examine existing biosignal world models through two requirements for intervention use: a genuine action and evidence of its causal effect. We identify three fundamental bottlenecks rooted in physiology: Temporal Latency, the variable delay between an action and its observable effect; System Openness, the influence of drivers beyond the modelled intervention; and Endogenous Dynamics, the system's ongoing evolution without that intervention. Drawing on published evidence, we outline corresponding research directions and propose an Intervention-Effect Validation Checklist to guide evaluation. The aim is to help the biosignal community realise the core promise of world models by learning the latent mechanisms that govern physiological evolution and responses to interventions.

title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
abstract: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.
comment: Experiment one presented at the 48th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society as a full paper talk in "Collective Intelligence."

title: Modeling the Microenvironmental Dynamics of Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma in Lacrimal Gland with Treatment Intervention
abstract: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the lacrimal gland is a rare and extremely life threatening malignant tumor with a high risk of recurrence and poor long-term outcomes. On the other hand, due to its complex molecular dynamics and low incidence rate, treatment strategies are very limited. In this study, a mathematical model is developed based on the biological phenomena of the tumor microenvironment using nonlinear ordinary differential equations. It is analyzed both analytically and numerically. According to the findings, the growth of tumor cells is associated with the depletion of oxygen and nutrients, while severe hypoxia promotes the development of abnormal blood vessels and makes tumor control more difficult. Surgery and postoperative radiotherapy have been considered as treatment strategies, and we have observed that surgery alone may not be sufficient to prevent the regrowth of residual tumor cells. In addition, postoperative radiotherapy provides better control of the residual tumor burden, particularly when the remaining tumor cells have higher radiosensitivity. Furthermore, different radiotherapy interruption scenarios have been investigated, and the results indicate that longer gaps between radiotherapy doses can adversely affect the overall treatment response, leading to increased overall toxicity and a higher number of residual tumor cells at the end of the observation period. Consequently, our results suggest that postoperative radiotherapy after surgery, combined with adequate radiosensitivity of the residual tumor cells and adherence to the prescribed treatment schedule without prolonged interruptions, may reduce the risk of tumor recurrence and potentially improve long term survival.

title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning
abstract: The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, despite divergence from their natural language training data. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

title: Functional and structural profiling of circulation via genetically encoded modular fluorescent probes.
abstract: Sustained labeling of fluids is crucial for their investigation in animal models. Here, we introduce a mouse line (Alb-mSc-ST), where blood and interstitial fluid are labeled with the red fluorescent protein mScarlet and SpyTag. The SpyTag-SpyCatcher technology is exploited to monitor circulating fluid properties by biosensors or detect blood-brain barrier disruption. This approach represents a valuable tool for studying vascular structure, permeability and microenvironment in body organs in vivo.

title: The Roads Not Taken: The Neural Dynamics of Lexical Alternatives During Free Language Production
abstract: Human language allows multiple ways to express the same thought, raising the possibility that several lexical candidates are activated in parallel before a single word is selected for articulation. While their co-activation is assumed by computational models of word production, until recently, there has been no practical way to estimate the identity of these candidates in unconstrained speech, nor to directly probe their representation in neural activity. Here, we combined high-density electrocorticography recorded during real-world conversation with context-sensitive large language model (LLM) to characterize, for the first time, how these lexical candidates are represented in the brain. We focus on the candidates which remain unsaid, referred to as the "alternatives", by only using samples where the LLM predictions do not include the produced word. We provide evidence for three computational principles of the neural dynamics of lexical alternatives: (1) multiple lexical alternatives to each word in conversation are distinctly represented in neural activity prior to articulation; (2) the set of lexical alternatives is rapidly updated from one word to the next; and (3) alternatives to future words are represented along with alternatives to the upcoming word. Together, these findings reveal that spontaneous speech production is supported by a broad, dynamically evolving and forward-looking set of lexical alternatives, providing a neural account of how the brain prepares not only the words that are spoken, but also those that remain unsaid.

title: Understanding neural circuit principles for representation learning through joint-embedding predictive architectures
abstract: Whether tracking prey or evading a predator, an animal's survival depends on both identifying objects in the environment and anticipating how they will move. To guide behavior, the brain must therefore extract information about object identities and their dynamics from entangled sensory inputs. How it accomplishes this feat remains an open question. Classical predictive coding theories propose that this ability arises by comparing predicted sensory signals with actual inputs and reducing the associated prediction errors. While such models capture important aspects of cortical computation, they typically focus on faithfully predicting sensory input and do not explicitly address how abstract, untangled representations of objects and their dynamics emerge solely through experience. Here, we develop a theory of representation learning in neural circuits that shifts the focus from prediction in the input space to prediction in representation space, without relying on external supervision or labeled data. Specifically, we introduce recurrent predictive learning (RPL), a recurrent joint-embedding predictive architecture inspired by self-supervised learning, that learns abstract representations of object identity and their dynamics and predicts future object motion from continuous sensory streams. While local learning rules alone can learn invariant object identity, we find that capturing object dynamics requires a circuit that explicitly generates and minimizes internal prediction-error signals. Crucially, the model learns sequence representations that resemble successor-like representations observed in the human primary visual cortex. The model also develops abstract sequence representations comparable to those reported in the macaque prefrontal cortex. Finally, we demonstrate a hierarchical version of RPL and discuss possible mappings onto cortical microcircuits. Our work establishes a circuit-centric theory framework that provides new perspectives on how the brain may acquire an internal model of the world through experience.
author_corresponding_institution: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research

title: Environmental co-option of chromatin potential links prenatal hypoxia to persistent cortical circuit dysfunction
abstract: Transient prenatal hypoxia is associated with long-term neurodevelopmental impairment without overt structural brain injury, suggesting early regulatory disruptions precede detectable pathology. Whether these disruptions represent transient stress responses or redirect developmental programs remains unknown. Here, we combined single-nucleus RNA sequencing and chromatin accessibility profiling in the late-gestation mouse cortex immediately after transient hypoxia, capturing responses across more than 140,000 nuclei. Hypoxia induced a largely conserved transcriptional stress response across cell types, whereas chromatin accessibility showed more extensive, cell type-specific disruption. Developing glutamatergic neurons showed the strongest disruption of chromatin transcription coupling, with hypoxia-responsive distal regulatory regions associated with genes governing synaptic organization and neuronal excitability. Consistent with these chromatin-associated programs, juvenile offspring displayed reduced dendritic spine density and increased intrinsic excitability in cortical neurons. These results support a model in which transient hypoxia co-opts the developing epigenome's capacity to encode future transcriptional states before persistent circuit dysfunction emerges.
author_corresponding_institution: Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania

title: p70 ribosomal protein S6 Kinase (p70S6K) as a potential peripheral biomarker for autistic symptoms in 16p11.2 deletion and duplication syndromes
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) encompass cognitive, motor, and psychiatric manifestations that require extensive assessments spanning different clinical domains. Individuals with syndromes caused by micro-deletions and -duplications in the proximal region of 16p11.2 have increased likelihood of neurodevelopmental and mental health symptoms, as well as cardiometabolic disorder. However, considerable phenotypic variability complicates prediction of risk, disease trajectory and treatment response. The identification of biomarkers in easily accessible tissues, such as Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells (PBMCs), could help diagnosis and prognosis, yet remains an unmet clinical need. Converging evidence implicates dysregulation of ubiquitous signalling pathways, including ERK and mTOR cascades, in altered protein synthesis across NDDs of both idiopathic and genetic origin. Here, using a hypothesis-driven approach, we examined candidate peripheral biomarkers in individuals with 16p11.2 proximal deletion and duplication syndromes. We established increased psychopathology and cognitive deficits in individuals with 16p11.2 deletion and duplication syndromes, compared to sibling controls. Furthermore, we identified a significant reduction of p70 S6 kinase (p70S6K) levels in PBMCs across both genotypes compared to controls. Notably, the magnitude of p70S6K reduction correlated with the severity of autistic symptoms independent of CNV genotype. In contrast, MAPK3/ERK1 protein levels mirrored the gene dosage, showing increased expression in individuals with the duplication and reduced levels in those with the deletion. These findings suggest that peripheral alterations in p70S6K may relate to variation in autism-related traits within individuals with 16p11.2 deletion and duplication syndromes, indicating that it may repreesent a potential biomarker of autism-associated symptom severity in this genetically at-risk group.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Biology and Biotechnology, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy

title: Pupil Dynamics Reflect Uncertainty-Driven Adjustments of Probability Learning
abstract: Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain's ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.
author_corresponding_institution: CEA Paris-Saclay Center - Fontenay-aux-Roses Site: Commissariat a l'energie atomique et aux energies alternatives Site de Fontenay-aux-Roses

title: Sparse Stimulus Generation Improves Reverse Correlation Efficiency and Interpretability
abstract: Reverse correlation is a widely-used and well-established method for probing latent perceptual representations in which subjects render subjective preference responses to ambiguous stimuli. Stimuli are purposefully designed to have no direct relationship with the target representation (e.g., they are randomly-generated), a property which makes each individual stimulus minimally informative toward reconstructing the target, and often difficult to interpret for subjects. As a result, a large number of stimulus-response pairs must be gathered from a given subject in order for reconstructions to be of sufficient quality, making the task fatiguing. Recent work has demonstrated that the number of trials needed can be substantially reduced using a compressive sensing framework that incorporates the assumption that the target representation can be sparsely represented in some basis into the reconstruction process. Here, we introduce an alternative method that incorporates the sparsity assumption directly into stimulus generation, which holds promise not only for improving efficiency, but also for improving the interpretability of stimuli from subject's perspective. We develop this new method as a mathematical variation of the compressive sensing approach, before conducting one simulation study and two human subjects experiments to assess the benefits of this method to reconstruction quality, sample size efficiency, and subjective interpretability. Results show that sparse stimulus generation improves all three of these areas relative to conventional reverse correlation approaches, and also relative to compressive sensing in most conditions.

title: Default Mode Network Connectivity Is Associated with Capture by Distractors Assigned to Learned Spatial Regularities
abstract: Salient distractors interfere with visual search, but observers can learn to filter out distractors that occur frequently and in predictable locations. We examined whether within-default-mode-network (DMN) task-run connectivity was associated with distractor capture and its location-dependent modulation in task-fMRI data from two groups in which either orientation or color distractors carried a spatial-probability bias. Higher within-DMN connectivity was associated with greater distractor capture by the biased distractor dimension, which was also the most frequent distractor type, whereas capture by the unbiased dimension was essentially unrelated to connectivity. A hierarchical trial-level model also showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling for the biased than for the unbiased dimension when both were evaluated under the same frequent-/rare-region weighting. DMN connectivity was also associated with spatial-probability learning, indexed by the rare-minus-frequent reaction-time difference on biased-dimension trials, but this association was closely tied to overall capture. When the physical distractor dimension was held constant, orientation showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling when it carried the spatial bias; in contrast, the corresponding color comparison remained uncertain. The broader network analyses provided converging support for this DMN-distractor-capture coupling pattern. Higher DMN connectivity was thus not associated with poorer performance in general, but with less effective filtering of the distractor that the task set was tuned to suppress. This pattern is consistent with a DMN state that interferes with implementing the optimal task set.

title: Clutter does not affect the spatial tuning of * category representations in human object-selective cortex *
abstract: Natural vision is frequently impaired when the visual field is crowded with multiple competing objects. One common interpretation of this clutter interference is that it originates from the large, position-tolerant receptive fields found in high-level visual cortex, which hinder the isolation of a target from its spatial surround. One way the visual system might counteract this interference is by relying on more localized object representations that are less prone to interference from objects at other locations and that are known to be prevalent also in higher-level visual cortex. If object encoding under clutter indeed uses more localized representations, then classifiers trained to recognize objects from one region of the visual field should generalize less well to other regions of the visual field in the presence of clutter compared to isolated objects. Here we tested this by measuring participants' brain signals with fMRI while they viewed objects presented either alone or within cluttered arrays. Consistent with prior work, category decoding accuracy was significantly reduced in clutter. However, we found that even classifiers trained directly on cluttered arrays generalize robustly across spatial positions, comparable to classifiers trained on isolated objects. This finding challenges the idea that clutter preferentially disrupts position-tolerant representations.
author_corresponding_institution: Bernstein Center for Computational Neuroscience Berlin

title: Astrocytes in the Dentate Gyrus Shift the Equilibrium from Pattern Separation to Pattern Completion and Inhibit Fear Extinction
abstract: Pattern separation and pattern completion are core hippocampal computations linked to memory interference and overgeneralization in many neuropsychiatric disorders and to mnemonic discrimination deficits in neurodegenerative conditions. Astrocytes are increasingly recognized as important integrators and modulators of neuronal activity as many studies have shown changes in animal behavior and neural circuits induced by manipulation of astrocytic activity. The role of astrocytes in the dentate gyrus for learning and memory is, however, largely unknown. To investigate the functional significance of astrocytic activity in the dentate gyrus, we expressed the calcium extruding pump hPMCA2w/b (CalEx), resulting in inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity, the Gq-coupled receptor hM3Dq, or the Gi-coupled receptor hM4Di, allowing chronic activation of Gq- and Gi-dependent pathways by a designer drug, in dentate gyrus astrocytes. Our main finding is that inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity by CalEx resulted in improved pattern separation and impaired pattern completion. In -vivo calcium imaging revealed that CalEx expression in astrocytes altered the neuronal activity pattern in dentate gyrus neurons with an overall inhibitory effect. This suggests that in the dentate gyrus astrocytes promote the activity of these neurons. Furthermore, chronic activation of hM4Di resulted in impaired between-session fear extinction while chronic activation of hM3Dq resulted in impaired within-session fear extinction and improved pattern separation learning over multiple days, suggesting that activation of astrocytic activity enhances mechanistically separable forms of fear extinction in a Gq- or Gi-pathway-specific manner. Our findings reveal that dentate gyrus astrocytic calcium shifts the balance between pattern separation and pattern completion towards pattern completion and thus modulates an essential neuronal functional output of the dentate gyrus. Chronic activation of astrocytes inhibits fear extinction, and thus also affects management of memory interference. Our findings imply that astrocytic modulation may be beneficial to treat cognitive deficits in disorders in which overgeneralization is a problem.

title: Cerebral hemodynamics and cytochrome c oxidase in hypoxic-ischemic rabbit fetuses
abstract: Background: Understanding fetal brain responses to hypoxia-ischemia is of growing interest, as it remains unclear to what extent these responses differ from those of newborns and whether developmental adaptations during gestation contribute to such differences. Materials and methods: Using a combination of broadband near-infrared spectroscopy (bNIRS) and diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS), we measured brain microvascular oxygen saturation (StO2), total hemoglobin concentration (THC), relative cerebral blood flow (rCBF), and the oxidation state of cytochrome c oxidase (oxCCO) during an acute ischemic challenge in the brains of five rabbit fetuses in utero. Simultaneous measurements were acquired from four control fetuses located in the contralateral uterine horn. Results: During the hypoxia-ischemia phase, we observed a rapid reduction of CBF (47% +/- 29%) and StO2, (from 64.7% +/- 1.5% at baseline to 40.6% +/- 2.0%) together with an increase of oxCCO (3.7 uM +/- 0.5 uM). Conclusion: The simultaneous increase in oxCCO and decrease in rCBF and StO2 during hypoxia-ischemia reveals a cerebral response pattern that differs from that commonly reported in the newborn brain. These findings support the hypothesis that unique developmental adaptations influence fetal cerebral metabolism during hypoxic-ischemic stress.

title: Suzetrigine-evoked analgesia is potentiated by Nav1.7 null-related opioid mechanisms.
abstract: The genetic evidence for an essential role of sodium channel Nav1.7 in human pain conditions is compelling. Unfortunately, potent selective channel blockers of Nav1.7 are not useful analgesics because they have deleterious side effects, particularly on the autonomic nervous system. Here we have evaluated the downstream mechanisms induced by Nav1.7 loss in utero. Nav1.1 compensates for loss of Nav1.7 in sensory neurons and antisense Nav1.1 oligonucleotides diminish excitability in Nav1.7 embryonic null sensory neurons. Enhanced endogenous opioid signalling contributes substantially to analgesia. This is linked to altered gene expression that potentiates opioid signalling through lowered levels of proteins that terminate G-protein signalling (RGS4 and RGS8). There is also enhanced opioid drive through increased enkephalin levels linked to lowered sodium levels in Nav1.7 null neurons. Opioid signalling is the main driver of analgesia, but enhanced potassium channel expression (KCNC4 KCNK2, KCNMB2, KCNAB3) all implicated in pain control, may also contribute to the small level of naloxone-resistant analgesia. These findings suggest a potential new route to analgesia, through mimicking the events at Nav1.7 null sensory neuron terminals. Here we demonstrate potentiation of suzetrigine-evoked analgesia with RGS antagonists alone or in combination with normally inactive doses of morphine in formalin-evoked pain and CFA-induced inflammatory pain. Intriguingly, no analgesia is observed with acute pain. Cancer pain is under investigation. These data are of potential clinical interest.

title: Single Cell Proteomics reveals partial uncoupling of the Glycerol-3-Phosphate shuttle to compensate for Electron Transport Chain dysfunction in Alexander Disease GFAP mutations
abstract: Alexander disease (AxD) is a rare genetic leukodystrophy caused by dominant mutations in the gene coding for the astrocytic intermediate filament protein Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP). Understanding disease mechanisms is complicated by the fact that mutant GFAP promotes further GFAP accumulation, making it difficult to distinguish mutation-specific effects from those caused by elevated GFAP levels. Here, we performed mass spectrometry-based single cell proteomics to investigate proteomic alterations associated with increasing levels of wildtype GFAP and a common AxD-causing mutant GFAP R239C. By analyzing individual cells spanning a broad range of GFAP expression levels, we separated dosage-dependent effects from mutation-specific responses. Cells expressing high levels of wildtype GFAP increasingly resembled R239C-expressing cells at the proteomic level, supporting a role for GFAP accumulation in disease pathogenesis. In contrast, mutant GFAP specifically correlated with increased mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes and remodeling of the proteasome tailored toward ATP- and ubiquitin-independent degradation of oxidized proteins. Integration with proteomics data from patient-derived cortical organoids revealed increased abundance of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins and respiratory chain assembly factors without corresponding changes in mitochondrially encoded proteins, suggesting impaired electron transport chain (ETC) assembly. Consistent with this, AxD cells displayed reduced oxygen consumption, increased glycolytic activity, enhanced utilization of the cytosolic part of the glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) shuttle, and accumulation of triacylglycerides and lipid droplets. We propose that ETC dysfunction promotes partial uncoupling of the G3P shuttle, allowing sustained regeneration of cytosolic NAD to support glycolysis while diverting G3P toward lipid synthesis and storage. By regenerating NAD through the G3P shuttle rather than lactate fermentation, AxD astrocytes may sustain glycolytic flux while preserving lactate production, an important metabolic substrate for neighboring neurons. Together, our findings identify ETC dysfunction as a central feature of AxD and suggest that metabolic adaptation through the G3P shuttle links mitochondrial dysfunction to glycolytic reprogramming and lipid accumulation. More broadly, these results provide new insight into how astrocyte dysfunction drives molecular pathways implicated in neurodegeneration.

title: Nicotinic modulation of frontal circuits breaks the cycle of attentional performance failure
abstract: The ability to recover from consecutive failures is critical for adaptive behavior, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. In vivo screening of neuromodulatory inputs onto frontal-sensory cognitive control circuit identified a frontal cholinergic mechanism that counteracts lapses in attentional engagement following repeated errors. Cholinergic input from the basal forebrain to the frontal cortex was necessary and sufficient to restore performance after errors, specifically after repeated-but not after a single-failure. This effect was mediated by 7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in frontal-sensory cortical neurons, which sustained cortical circuit activity and frontal-sensory cortical oscillations during attentional engagement. Targeted optogenetic activation of these frontal-sensory neurons disrupted cycles of attentional performance failure and reinstated behavioral performance in a mouse model of neuropsychiatric syndrome. These findings reveal a circuit-level mechanism of cholinergic control that confers cognitive resilience under conditions of persistent failure.
author_corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

title: Large-scale all-optical electrophysiology links excitability and connectivity to circuit dynamics in vivo
abstract: To understand neural computations, one would like to relate circuit dynamics to neuronal intrinsic excitability and connectivity. We developed tools for large-scale all-optical electrophysiology and applied them to approximately 300 layer 1 interneurons per mouse in vivo. Across two mice, targeted stimulation and voltage imaging identified 1,469 inhibitory and 5,752 directed electrical connections among 14,312 tested pairs. Presynaptic identity was more strongly associated with inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) amplitude, whereas postsynaptic identity was more strongly associated with IPSP decay time. Gap junctional and synaptic interactions had distinct spatiotemporal kernels, with corresponding signatures in spontaneous activity. Excitability measured under optogenetic stimulus predicted spiking responses to subthreshold voltage, depolarization rate, and spike history during spontaneous firing. Genetic subtypes also showed different behavioral-state-dependent voltage-to-spike relationships despite similar population-average subthreshold voltages. These measurements link cellular properties and pairwise interactions to spontaneous circuit dynamics, establishing an approach for functional circuit mapping in vivo.

title: Beyond the attractor: closed-loop stimulation design for learning multistable neural dynamics
abstract: Online identification of nonlinear dynamical systems faces two challenges. Noisy, partial observations make the latent state difficult to estimate. Local attractors can also keep passive trajectories in regions that reveal little about the unknown dynamics. Both challenges commonly arise in closed-loop neural experiments where stimulation must be chosen from noisy spike counts, while neural activity may remain near a stable state unless stimulation drives it elsewhere. We address this problem by actively selecting inputs to collect informative observations during the experiment. We introduce PALDI (Planning-based Active Latent Dynamics Identification), which combines extended-Kalman state prediction, single-step Laplace state updates, blockwise Gaussian parameter updates, and finite-horizon planning. Its parameter expected-information-gain surrogate combines dynamics sensitivity with state Fisher information and discounts apparent parameter information when latent states are uncertain. We compare PALDI with nonadaptive inputs, a myopic policy, and two active baselines: the one-step D-optimal method FLEX and receding-horizon curiosity with uncertainty sampling. On a bistable Wilson-Cowan model of excitatory and inhibitory populations, PALDI approaches the true-model reference and remains strongest as the observation signal-to-noise ratio decreases or the readout geometry becomes biased. We then test identification in a spiking decision network where we use a reduced dynamics and observation model to approximate the data-generating process. PALDI reaches a median held-out prediction R2 of 0.90, close to a fitted reference, and its model gives the highest change-of-mind success among identification policies. Information-guided finite-horizon planning is a practical strategy for identifying neural circuit dynamics with closed-loop stimulation.

title: An integrated multi-omic atlas of the choroid plexus highlights conserved molecular programs of epithelial function
abstract: The choroid plexus (ChP) is a specialized epithelial tissue responsible for production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), maintenance of the blood-CSF barrier and regulation of CSF-borne signaling factors. However, despite the ChP's central role in CSF homeostasis, conserved molecular programs of ChP epithelial function across species and conditions remain incompletely defined. In this study, we integrated eight mouse and human single-cell/nucleus RNA-seq datasets to build a multi-species ChP atlas capturing major epithelial, stromal, vascular, and immune populations. Cross-dataset differential expression identified a conserved epithelial gene program encompassing ion transport, barrier function, ciliogenesis, and secretory signaling, while prioritizing understudied genes including CLIC6 and VAT1L. Co-expression network analysis resolved conserved epithelial meta-programs, and transcription factor regulatory inference identified OTX2, MSX1, and GLIS3 among conserved regulators of epithelial gene expression. We also generated a novel Visium HD spatial transcriptomic atlas of mouse fourth-ventricle ChP to orthogonally validate epithelial modules. Lastly, cross-tissue analyses revealed substantial transcriptional overlap between ChP and retinal pigment epithelium, including shared epithelial genes and OTX2-associated regulatory relationships. Together, these findings define conserved molecular programs of ChP epithelial specialization, nominate candidate regulators for functional investigation, and provide an integrated cross-species and spatial resource for studying ChP physiology.

title: Induction of interhemispheric visual plasticity by paired associative stimulation
abstract: Unveiling the plastic mechanisms of the primary visual cortex (V1) is crucial for understanding how visual processing can change and adapt, ultimately informing interventions to promote functional recovery following visual system damage. Paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocols can induce associative plasticity within the human V1. However, previous paradigms used full-field visual stimulation, engaging both hemispheres simultaneously, leaving unclear whether plasticity can be selectively targeted to a single visual pathway and whether it can modulate the non-stimulated hemisphere. Across three experiments in healthy participants, we investigated the neurophysiological, behavioural, and interhemispheric outcomes of a novel lateralized visual PAS protocol (vPAS). Pattern-reversal checkerboards were presented in a single visual hemifield and time-locked to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses delivered over the contralateral V1. Experiment 1 assessed neurophysiological effects by recording hemifield-lateralized visual-evoked potentials (VEPs) and testing three inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs: 75, 100, and 125 ms) between vPAS-paired stimuli. Experiment 2 evaluated perceptual changes in contrast detection, while Experiment 3 examined vPAS hemispheric specificity and aftereffects on interhemispheric visuomotor transfer. Only the 75-ms ISI consistently modulated visual processing in the non-conditioned hemisphere, reducing N75 amplitude and improving contrast detection for visual stimuli presented contralateral to the TMS side. Longer ISIs were not effective. Furthermore, this protocol altered interhemispheric transfer exclusively when the left, but not the right, V1 was targeted during vPAS. In conclusion, lateralized vPAS induces timing-dependent changes beyond the stimulated cortex, suggesting that associative plasticity can engage contralateral visual circuits and modulate visual processing.

title: Impaired Control Symptoms in Alcohol Use Disorder Show Convergent Associations Across Behavioral and Neural Markers of Inhibitory Control and Drinking Behavior
abstract: Background: Deficits in inhibitory control are considered a central feature of alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet behavioral and neuroimaging findings have been inconsistent. One potential explanation is the marked heterogeneity of AUD, which encompasses multiple symptom dimensions that may differ in their underlying neurocognitive mechanisms. In this study, we investigated whether behavioral and neural markers of inhibitory control are associated with specific DSM-5 AUD symptom domains. Methods: A total of 589 participants (432 with non-treatment seeking AUD, 157 controls) completed a Stop-Signal Task (SST) during fMRI. Associations between DSM-5 symptom domains (impaired control over alcohol use, risky use, social problems, physical dependence) and SST performance, inhibition-related brain activation, and alcohol consumption were examined. Real-life drinking behavior was additionally assessed over 12 months using ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Results: Greater impaired control symptom severity was associated with poorer performance on go trials and diminished post-error slowing during SST. At the neural level, higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with reduced activation across fronto-insular, parietal, cingulate, supplementary motor, and cerebellar regions. In contrast, other symptom domains showed little to no associations with inhibition-related behavioral or neural measures. Higher impaired control symptom severity was associated with greater alcohol consumption across questionnaire-based and EMA-based assessments. Conclusions: In this large cohort, altered behavioral performance and recruitment of inhibition-related brain regions in the SST was selectively linked to impaired control symptoms. These findings highlight the importance of symptom-based approaches for understanding heterogeneity in addiction and may inform the development of more targeted interventions.

title: CLEAR-FORCE: A reservoir computing framework for closed-loop brain stimulation
abstract: Electrical stimulation of brain activity has emerged as a key therapeutic intervention for neurological diseases. The success of these approaches relies on precisely tuned stimulation parameters. A major challenge is that these parameters should ideally be adjusted in real-time based on changes in brain activity. Closed-loop controllers address this challenge by monitoring brain activity and adapting stimulation according to ongoing changes in neural dynamics. While machine learning has been helpful in this context, closed-loop controllers typically do not adapt in real-time to fluctuations in brain activity. Here, we propose a novel framework based on reservoir computing to train a closed-loop, real-time neural controller. This approach, termed CLEAR-FORCE, trains the output weights of a recurrent network based on a combination of target signals and feedback from brain activity. Two series of simulations were performed, where the controller was successful at (1) inducing neural oscillations in a population of spiking neurons and (2) suppressing pathological oscillations. This framework provides a promising avenue for the implementation of neural controllers in low-powered, real-time, and adaptive hardware that harnesses machine learning for the personalized treatment of brain disorders.

title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models
abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

title: Olfactory Deficits and Structural Anomalies of the Peripheral Olfactory System in 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
abstract: Background: Approximately 25% of individuals with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) develop a psychotic disorder, and the syndrome shares key neurodevelopmental features with psychosis in the general population. The olfactory system develops early in utero, providing a window into gestational disruptions relevant to psychosis risk. We hypothesized that 22q11DS would show impairments in olfactory function and structural anomalies of the olfactory system relative to psychosis spectrum (PS) youth without a known genetic syndrome and typically developing controls (TD). Methods: Participants included individuals with 22q11DS (n=101), PS (n=56), and TD (n=52). Sinonasal symptoms, odor identification, and discrimination (Sniffin' Sticks) behaviorally. Structural 3T MRI measured olfactory bulb volume, sulcus depth, and sulcus length. Sample sizes vary per analysis. Results: Relative to TD, 22q11DS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p<.001), lower odor identification (p<.001), and lower odor discrimination (p<.001). PS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p<.001) and marginally lower odor identification (p=.06), but no discrimination deficit. Olfactory bulb volume was significantly smaller in 22q11DS versus TD (p=.007, r=.39); PS showed a non-significant trend (p=.07). Olfactory sulcus depth (p=.52) and length (p=.82) did not differ across groups. Conclusions: 22q11DS is associated with elevated sinonasal burden, robust olfactory identification and discrimination deficits exceeding those of PS and reduced olfactory bulb volume. The co-occurrence of functional deficits and reduced bulb volume without sulcal anomalies may distinguish the 22q11DS olfactory phenotype from that of PS. These hypothesis-generating findings are consistent with partially dissociable neurodevelopmental mechanisms and support the utility of 22q11DS as a genetic model for psychosis risk.

title: Motor effort biases perceptual decisions through later-stage evidence accumulation rather than early sensory-attentional processing
abstract: Motor effort has been shown to bias perceptual decisions toward less effortful choices, but it remains unknown whether this bias already takes effect during the early stages of decision formation through preparatory attentional allocation or sensory processing, or during later-stage evidence accumulation preceding response execution. This study investigated when motor effort becomes integrated into decision formation by focusing on the temporal evolution of neural processing during perceptual decision-making. While 64-channel EEG was recorded, twenty-four healthy adults performed an orientation discrimination task in which two Gabor patches appeared simultaneously in the left and right visual hemifield and decisions were reported using two pressure-sensitive response buttons requiring different levels of force. We found that motor effort modulated EEG activity at both the preparatory and later decision stages: pre-stimulus alpha power was reduced over the occipito-parietal cortex contralateral to the low-effort option, and mean centro-parietal positivity (CPP) amplitude preceding response execution was greater over centro-parietal cortex for low-effort choices, while leaving early sensory representations intact as indicated by no differences in P1 or N1 amplitude following stimulus onset. Trial-by-trial CPP amplitude preceding response execution increased with the likelihood of selecting the low-effort option, whereas the pre-stimulus alpha modulation was not associated with behavioral decision bias. These findings suggest that motor effort biases perceptual decisions primarily during later-stage evidence accumulation, thereby providing insight into the neural basis of embodied perceptual decision making.

title: Optimizing Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation: The Effects of Pulse Parameters on Corticospinal Excitability
abstract: Objective. Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is a repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) protocol used in clinical settings to alleviate symptoms of psychiatric disorders. Although the pulse parameters currently used in iTBS have remained unchanged since the first treatments, recent controllable TMS devices allow for the personalization of pulse shape and duration, opening the possibility of testing the efficacy of other pulse parameters in modulating corticospinal excitability (CSE). Methods. In a repeated-measures design, changes in CSE were induced by the administration of iTBS over the left primary motor cortex under three different conditions: long bidirectional pulse (L-Bi), long quasi-unidirectional pulse (L-QU), and a control short quasi-unidirectional pulse (S-QU). We assessed TMS-induced motor evoked potentials before and up to 70 minutes after iTBS. We hypothesized that L-QU pulses would induce greater facilitation than other conditions. Results. A mixed linear model showed that all conditions induced increased MEPs compared to baseline. However, the L-Bi pulse led to a larger and more sustained MEP increase than both unidirectional pulses, while the S-QU pulse appeared less effective in modulating CSE. We observed large within- and between-subject variability in responsiveness to the iTBS protocols. Conclusion. These results suggest that L-Bi pulses in iTBS protocols are more potent than unidirectional pulses in inducing CSE changes in the cortex of healthy adults. The individual variability in response to iTBS and the potential clinical relevance of these findings are discussed.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for subject-specific recovery of travelling-wave structure in resting-state fMRI
abstract: Resting-state BOLD fluctuations show reproducible spatiotemporal propagation that is not accounted for by conventional zero-lag functional connectivity. Travelling wave analyses based on phase gradients or statistical decomposition have problems when multiple wave generators overlap or when wave origins have to be localized. This work introduces a wave-informed physics-informed neural network that represents the parcellated BOLD signal as a superposition of seven spatially extended damped travelling wave generators, each periodically re-excited at its own characteristic frequency and fixed at initialization to one of the seven canonical Schaefer resting-state networks. A soft anatomical prior derived from each subject's diffusion-tensor structural connectivity is included to encode the hypothesis that white-matter pathways constrain wave direction. The pipeline is validated on synthetic data by three simulation studies, creating the operating envelope, and then applied to 41 cognitively normal participants of the ADNI 3 cohort. A within-subject ablation showed that mean alignment between recovered wave directions and underlying white matter geometry increased by a small but statistically detectable amount when using the structural prior (one-sidedWilcoxon signed-rank, p = 0.026), with exploratory network-level effects most evident in the visual, dorsal-attention, and salience/ventral-attention networks. The contribution is a network-anchored parametric inverse method returning subject-specific propagation descriptors from short resting-state scans.

title: Syntaxin-1 and syntaxin binding protein 1-1 are required for planarian behavior and brain regeneration
abstract: Background: Nervous system regeneration requires creation of new neurons and their integration into new and existing networks. How new neurons find their targets and reconnect in the environment of regenerating tissue remains a major gap in knowledge. The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea is well suited to the study of neural regeneration due to the remarkable ability of planarians to regenerate their entire body, including the nervous system. However, we have not yet been able to explore synaptogenesis in regeneration using planarians due to a lack of tools to study synapses. Here we investigate potential players in planarian synapse, focusing on the conserved syntaxin protein family, which functions in neurotransmitter vesicle fusion at the synapse. Results: We found that reduction of either syntaxin-1 (stx1) or syntaxin-binding protein 1-1 (stxbp1-1) decreased locomotion and impeded brain regeneration, specifically in synapse-rich regions. Conclusions: Our observations support STX-1 and STXBP1-1 as bona fide synapse components, providing a starting point for studies neuronal connectivity during homeostatic remodeling and regeneration.

title: ISL1 is required for the terminal differentiation and maintenance of Starburst Amacrine Cells
abstract: During mammalian nervous system development, multipotent progenitor cells differentiate into hundreds of distinct neuronal subtypes. Neuronal subtype terminal differentiation is regulated by transcription factors that directly control the acquisition and maintenance of terminal identity. Using the mouse retina as a model system, we show that the transcription factor ISL1 is required for the terminal differentiation and maintenance of starburst amacrine cells (SACs), the sole cholinergic neuron subtype in the retina. We conditionally deleted Isl1 selectively from amacrine and horizontal cell precursors, allowing us to assess its cell-autonomous role in SAC development without disrupting its critical function in bipolar cell and retinal ganglion cell development. We find that ISL1 is not required for initial SAC specification but is required for their terminal differentiation. Isl1-deficient SACs retain a GABAergic amacrine cell identity but fail to adopt many SAC-specific features including expression of genes required for cholinergic transmission. In the absence of ISL1, SACs fail to migrate properly, with both OFF- and ON- SACs localizing to the inner nuclear layer. Deletion of Isl1 from post-migratory SACs at later stages of development revealed that it is also required for maintaining SAC identity and proper dendrite stratification. Loss of Isl1 from SACs ultimately caused abnormal development of the direction selective circuit. Together, these findings establish that ISL1 is required for the induction and maintenance of SAC-specific identity from a generic amacrine state.

title: Not all memory declines with age: Neural correlates of implicit associative memory in younger and older adults.
abstract: While explicit associative memory declines with age, implicit associative memory remains preserved. Few studies have examined the neural basis of implicit associative memory in aging, and it remains unclear whether the hippocampus is required as it is more often associated with explicit associative memory. While undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging, young and old adults completed a speeded object categorization task in which they viewed pictured objects with superimposed words. Implicit memory was tested by presenting intact (original pairs) and rearranged pairs (items previously presented, but not together) from encoding while participants did the same categorization task. Associative priming was defined as faster reaction times (behavioural associative priming) and less activation for intact than rearranged pairs at retrieval (neural associative priming). Whole-brain analyses revealed neural associative priming in occipitotemporal and frontal regions that did not differ by age. A region of interest analysis (using subject-specific masks of medial temporal lobe regions) showed that only older adults had greater posterior hippocampal activation to intact than rearranged items at test, though activation in the hippocampus did not relate to behavioural associative priming. In contrast, greater behavioural associative priming was related to greater neural associative priming in the perirhinal cortex in both age groups. Together, these findings suggest that implicit associative priming remains intact with age, possibly because it relies on additional processes outside the hippocampus such as perirhinal-dependent unitization.

title: Primary cilia facilitate GPCR neurotransmission through the canonical cAMP cascade
abstract: The primary cilium is increasingly recognized to be a discrete site for initiating neurotransmission through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), yet how such neurotransmission is propagated downstream remains unclear. A canonical pathway of downstream GPCR neurotransmission is the cyclic AMP (cAMP) / cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) cascade. While cAMP can be locally generated in cilia and produce important effects that are functionally compartmentalized there, neurotransmission through GPCRs must propagate to effectors outside of cilia. Thus, a prevailing current view is that ciliary neurotransmission is restricted to non-canonical, cAMP-dependent pathways. Revisiting this view, we show here that the primary cilium of striatal medium spiny neurons is a major site from which endogenous D1 dopamine receptors initiate cAMP and PKA activity elevations that propagate throughout the extraciliary cytoplasm. We also show that the primary cilium spatially aligns essentially this entire long-range signaling axis from intercalating with numerous dopaminergic axon varicosities that initiate neurotransmission to enforcing proximity with somatic PKA stores that are activated by cAMP downstream. Together, these results extend the concept of ciliary neurotransmission to dopaminergic signaling in striatal neurons and reveal that, in this system, the primary cilium facilitates rather than restricts neurotransmission through the canonical cAMP / PKA cascade.

title: Intersectional genetic targeting of molecularly distinct melanin-concentrating hormone neuron subpopulations reveals distinct and overlapping subcircuit architecture
abstract: The lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) coordinates crucial and innate behaviors through heterogeneous yet poorly understood neuronal populations and circuits. Neurons that produce melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH; encoded by the Pmch gene) are primarily localized in the LHA and contribute to feeding, sleep-wake regulation, memory, and reward-associated behaviors. Building on foundational anatomical studies, our single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the LHA identified markers distinguishing at least two transcriptionally distinct MCH subpopulations. These subpopulations are distinguished by the selective enrichment of the Tacr3 and Cartpt transcripts, with each comprising approximately half of the total MCH population. However, these subpopulations remain poorly understood owing to limited genetic targeting tools. We hypothesized that MCH neurons operate through functionally distinct, parallel subcircuits that exhibit unique neuroanatomical projections. In this study, we leveraged Pmch and Tacr3 expression to intersectionally dissociate these neurons into Type I MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3+) and Type II MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3-) subpopulations. We first validated a Tacr3-Flpo mouse line for the genetic targeting of the Type I MCH subpopulation. We then generated an intersectional Type I MCH neuron reporter line to visualize Type I axonal projections. In parallel, we injected a dual recombinase mouse line with the intersectional genetic targeting viruses, Conditional Viral Expression by Ribozyme Guided Degradation (ConVERGD), and identified overlapping and distinct projections by Type I and Type II MCH neurons using fluorescence microscopy, super-resolution imaging, and high-spatial resolution fiber mapping. Overall, these data establish the first subpopulation-resolved anatomical framework for molecularly distinct Type I and Type II MCH subcircuits, thus establishing a foundation for future circuit-level functional studies.

title: Astrocyte-Specific dsRNA-ADAR1 Signalling Links Innate Immunity to Complement Activation in Parkinson Disease
abstract: Background: Dysregulated innate immune activation is a key feature of Parkinson disease (PD), but the upstream triggers and cell-type-specific mechanisms remain unclear. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) has emerged as a potential driver of innate immune responses. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1), particularly its interferon-inducible p150 isoform, edits dsRNA to limit aberrant immune activation. Whether this dsRNA-ADAR1 axis contributes to neuroinflammation in PD in a cell-type-specific manner is unknown. Methods: We performed immunofluorescence on post-mortem cingulate cortex tissue from PD cases and controls to localise dsRNA, ADAR1 p150 and pathological alpha-synuclein protein. We integrated these findings with single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from three independent human brain datasets. An eight-module gene scoring framework was applied to assess dsRNA processing, sensing, and downstream innate immune pathways in neurons and astrocytes. Results: In PD cortex, the proportion of dsRNA-positive astrocytes was higher than in controls, whereas neuronal dsRNA positivity did not differ between groups. ADAR1 p150 positivity increased in both astrocytes and neurons, and the proportion of ADAR1 p150 positive astrocytes correlated with astrocytic -synuclein burden. Transcriptomic analyses showed that neurons were enriched for dsRNA editing and processing machinery, whereas astrocytes exhibited higher expression of dsRNA sensing pathways, innate immune responses, and transposable element control. While overall pathway activity did not differ between PD and controls after covariate adjustment, network analyses revealed cell-type-specific coupling patterns. Notably, complement gene expression showed a strong and selective association with dsRNA-related pathways in astrocytes, whereas interferon and NF-{kappa}B signalling were shared across cell types. In both cell types, ADAR1-associated gene programmes were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation and PD-related pathways. Conclusions: These findings identify astrocytes as a central site of relative dsRNA accumulation and ADAR1 p150 induction in the PD cortex. The selective coupling of dsRNA sensing to complement activation in astrocytes highlights a cell-type-specific innate immune pathway that is constitutively present rather than induced by disease. Together, our protein-level and network-level findings converge on a coherent and testable model in which a constitutive astrocytic circuit is engaged by disease-associated dsRNA accumulation, with potential relevance for disease progression and therapeutic targeting.

title: How aging reshapes implicit learning: behavioral and oscillatory evidence from an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm.
abstract: Most of everyday memory formation occurs without deliberate intent, yet the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding and their reorganization with age remain poorly understood. The present study investigated age-related changes in implicit learning using an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm (the Disjunctive Inference Implicit Learning Test, DIILT) in 31 younger and 35 older adults, paired with a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and a one-month delayed recognition measure. Behaviorally, younger adults rapidly acquired novel implicit associations across the learning phase, whereas older adults showed persistent reliance on familiar items and limited improvement for novel associations. Critically, both groups successfully retained novel associations after one month, with implicitly learned associations showing greater long-term stability than explicitly encoded ones regardless of age. At the neural level, younger adults exhibited early posterior theta engagement for novel compared to familiar items, which disappeared by the end of learning, consistent with novelty-driven associative encoding. Older adults showed no such theta modulation for novel items, pointing to reorganization of the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding. Theta dynamics predicted immediate recognition in younger adults but not in older adults who rather showed theta association with processing speed, suggesting an age-related shift from memory-specific binding to domain-general cognitive resource allocation, consistent with neural maintenance frameworks of cognitive aging. These findings demonstrate that implicit encoding produces durable memory traces across the lifespan but relies on reorganized oscillatory dynamics in aging, with implications for understanding how cognitive aging reshapes everyday memory formation.

title: A rapid, genetically-tractable human iPSC-derived model for studying tissue-resident macrophage biology in Alzheimer's and other diseases
abstract: Large-scale genetic and preclinical studies strongly implicate myeloid cells, particularly brain-resident macrophages, in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Efferocytic clearance of apoptotic cells and other cholesterol-rich cellular debris is a core macrophage function and represents an active area of AD research. However, human tissue-resident macrophages remain difficult to model in vitro as they acquire their transcriptional and functional identities in response to signals from their host tissue microenvironment. Many existing differentiation protocols mimic human brain macrophage developmental trajectories, but these protocols rely either on multi-step cytokine cocktails and lengthy differentiation or transduction of multiple transcription factors, both of which introduce variability and complicate genetic manipulation. To address these limitations, we developed a simplified protocol that generates high-purity (>90% CD45+CD11b+) human iPSC-derived macrophage-like cells (iMacs) from cryopreservable erythro-myeloid progenitor (EMP)-like intermediates in 19 days, including a final 7-day maturation step driven by macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) alone. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that iMacs show enrichment for phagocytic and lysosomal programs, processes integral to efferocytosis. At both the transcriptional and protein level, iMacs have higher expression of scavenger receptors such as CD36, CD163 and MRC1, and of AD risk genes such as TREM2. Functionally, iMacs show enhanced phagocytic uptake of diverse substrates relative to iPSC-derived microglia, including carboxylated latex beads, zymosan, amyloid-{beta} 1-42, and amyloid-{beta} 1-40, and exhibit expanded lysosomal mass. Robust TREM2 expression and signaling make iMacs a sensitive platform for interrogating TREM2 biology, with markedly higher phosphorylation of SYK and PLC{gamma}2 in response to TREM2 engagement compared to iPSC-derived microglia. iMacs also tolerate lipid-mediated siRNA transfection with high survival and knockdown efficiency, enabling rapid genetic perturbation of AD risk genes. Together, these features make iMacs a practical, scalable, and genetically tractable human macrophage model for studying the regulation and cell biology of core macrophage functions that are known to play critical roles in AD, aging, and other disorders.
author_corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

title: NE52-QQ57 attenuates post-ischemia protein phosphorylation in the mouse brain
abstract: Introduction: Cerebral ischemia induces a reduction in brain pH. GPR4, a proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptor is highly expressed in vascular endothelial cells. Pharmacological inhibition of GPR4 with NE52-QQ57 (NEQQ) reduces ischemia-induced blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and brain injury. To facilitate targeting GPR4 in vivo, it is important to better define the effect of NEQQ on post-ischemia signaling and the pharmacokinetics of NEQQ in vivo. Methods: We performed biochemical analysis following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). We used Liquid Chromatography-Mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to quantify the concentration of NEQQ in serum, brain, and peripheral tissues. Results: NEQQ administration decreased the phosphorylation of PKA substrates, PKC substrates, ERK1/2, and CREB. LC-MS/MS analysis detected NEQQ in both ipsilateral and contralateral hemisphere of the brain at 5 h and 24 h after reperfusion, demonstrating that NEQQ crosses the BBB. In peripheral tissues, NEQQ exhibited highest level in kidney and lowest in the heart. In sham controls, average serum concentrations were ~4 and 0.9 g/g at 5 and 24 h, respectively. Following tMCAO, ipsilateral brain exhibited higher levels as compared to the contralateral side at 5 h while the difference diminished at 24 h. Conclusions: NEQQ attenuated the ischemia-induced activation of multiple signaling pathways. NEQQ exhibited broad distribution in peripheral organs, and its brain level was sufficient for GPR4 inhibition at 24 h after injection. These findings support the use of NEQQ as a pharmacological inhibitor of GPR4-mediated signaling following ischemic stroke.

title: Intranasal L-MYC Neural Stem Cells Restore Neurovascular and Neuroimmune Homeostasis After TBI via CX3CL1 Upregulation and ICAM-1 Downregulation
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers persistent neuroimmune and neurovascular dysfunction that contributes to secondary brain injury and limits recovery. Here, we investigated whether a single intranasal dose of LMNSC01 could reprogram neuroinflammatory and neurovascular responses post TBI and whether these effects were conserved across biological sex. Immunocompetent male and female rats underwent a controlled cortical impact (CCI) or Sham surgery and 7 days later received a single bolus dose of LMNSC01 (6 x10^6 cells/dose) or vehicle. Integrated histological and transcriptomic analyses and multiplex tissue ELISA were used to characterize injury- and treatment-associated responses. CCI induced persistent but sex-dependent transcriptional changes. Male rats exhibited prominent innate immune, adhesion, extracellular matrix, and tissue remodeling responses, whereas females demonstrated broader activation of microglial, interferon, complement, MHC/antigen presentation, and humoral/adaptive immune pathways. LMNSC01 treatment reprogrammed these distinct injury states through partially sex-specific mechanisms. In males, LMNSC01 increased endogenous immune-regulatory mediators, including Il1rn, and reduced pathways associated with adhesion and immune cell trafficking. In females, treatment decreased expression of genes related to microglial, leukocyte, MHC/antigen presentation, cytokine, and adhesion pathways, and reduced macrophage- and CD45 positive cell signatures. Despite these sex-dependent transcriptional changes, LMNSC01 produced conserved protein changes in both sexes, reducing injury associated ICAM-1 and restoring CX3CL1 proteins, proposing a novel molecular mechanism of LMNSCs modulating endothelial activation and neuron-microglia communication post injury. Our study provides further insight into sex differences in responses to injury and treatment after TBI and highlights candidate repair mechanisms, supporting further development of LMNSC01 as a minimally invasive therapy for TBI.

title: From Intrinsic Topography to Cognitive Prediction: Benchmarking Approaches to Personalized Cortical Parcellation
abstract: Personalized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) adapts cortical parcellations to individual functional anatomy. Various methods have been proposed that differ in how they combine group-level information, spatial constraints, and individual functional data. Using the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset (N = 947), we compared five personalized parcellation methods and a standard group-level atlas. For each method, we calculated functional homogeneity, test-retest reliability, parcel contiguity, and inter-individual Dice overlap. Personalized parcellation methods generally yielded higher functional homogeneity and lower inter-individual Dice than the group atlas, while test-retest reliability of functional connectivity was high across methods. Parcel contiguity differed across methods: some approaches produced almost entirely contiguous parcels, whereas others frequently produced spatially disconnected components, indicating that the detection of candidate ectopic variants depends partly on the parcellation strategy. We also examined whether connectivity and topographic features were associated with and predicted general intelligence (g). Using structural equation modeling, intra-individual parcel size variability and inter-individual parcel size similarity derived from the hierarchical Bayesian method (gMSHBM) were positively associated with g, whereas no corresponding association survived correction for the other methods. Using kernel ridge regression, functional connectivity significantly predicted g, with the group atlas yielding the highest predictive accuracy, consistent with a potential advantage of cross-individual spatial correspondence for edge-wise prediction. Finally, we assessed robustness across four preprocessing pipelines. Although gMSHBM parcellations were not re-estimated, relative between-method patterns in several spatial characteristics were largely preserved. In contrast, brain-behavior associations involving time-series-derived features varied substantially with preprocessing, whereas parcel-size associations were more stable. We conclude that personalized parcellation approaches are associated with distinct trade-offs in spatial correspondence, topographic variability, and downstream predictive utility. The choice of parcellation strategy therefore affects both the properties of individualized maps and the brain-behavior information derived from them.

title: Identification of Synchronously Active Cells (ISAC) to study the activity of cell assemblies
abstract: Cell assemblies--groups of neurons that fire synchronously--are central to neuronal computation. Technological advances now permit the simultaneous recording of large neuronal populations; however, many existing cell assembly detection algorithms rely on simplified measures such as pairwise correlations, failing to capture higher-order synchrony and thereby missing a rich repertoire of assemblies present in the data. To address these limitations, we developed Identification of Synchronously Active Cells (ISAC), which performs a rigorous, iterative search across all recorded units, leveraging the full dimensionality of the dataset to detect groups that fire together above chance. Using simulated recordings with ground-truth assemblies of increasing complexity, we demonstrate that ISAC considerably outperforms currently used algorithms in identifying synchronously active cells. Finally, we show that applying ISAC to experimental recordings uncovers novel features of assembly formation and dynamics. The power and sensitivity of ISAC can thus enable insights that remain inaccessible with existing methods.
